title: Weekend Musings: The Houston Texans and the NFL world 25 Years Ago
summary: This past Friday marked the anniversary of one of the most seminal events in US History: The terrorist attacks that hit New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania. Nearly 3000 Americans killed, two of the largest buildings in the US destroyed, the command-and-control center of the US military damaged and the most powerful nation ground to […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 11: A detail of Uvalde Strong and 9/11 remembrance stickers on a Houston Texans helmet prior to the game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 11, 2022 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Bob Levey/Getty Images) | Getty Images This past Friday marked the anniversary of one of the most seminal events in US History: The terrorist attacks that hit New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania. Nearly 3000 Americans killed, two of the largest buildings in the US destroyed, the command-and-control center of the US military damaged and the most powerful nation ground to a practical halt. One could argue that this was the moment that the US entered the 21st century, and the events of that day would drive American actions for the next 25 years. The impacts are still felt to this day, and likely will continue to be felt for the foreseeable future. No aspect of American life was untouched by that day. Very much included in that was the world of pro sports. The NFL had just kicked off the 2001 season the weekend prior, and MLB was entering the stretch run for the drive to its postseason. However, the events of the morning of Sept 11 put those organizations on hold. MLB games did not take place. Given that Sept 11 was a Tuesday, the NFL apparently had time to figure out what they wanted to do (Thursday Night Games weren’t a regular thing at this point). Then, as now, the NFL ruled the sporting world in America. Other sports, like baseball, immediately cancelled/postponed games slated for that night, while trying to figure out when they would get back in business. The NFL faced two courses of action. On one hand, there was an argument for the league to play the scheduled games. A chance for America to escape into a much-needed distraction. Also, the thought that America could and would not be thwarted by any adversary, especially one that based their operations out of some mountain caves was unbearable. Security was a major concern, but America could ramp up its internal and external security measures to ensure that there would be no repeat at a stadium full of fans. Yet, the other side of the debate was just as strong. America reeled with shock and grief. Security upgrades were barely established for travel and industry. The stress of suddenly having to security massive stadiums filled with tens of thousands of people was hard to fathom. There was sense that the nation still needed time to grieve and that playing games in light of the worst attack against America since World War II was the wrong thing to do. Additionally, would the players that approached the games the weekend prior with passion and desire still have that fire to play in so short a time after Sept 11th? In particular, players from New York and Washington found themselves hardly able to focus enough to practice, much less get up for playing actual games. Most sporting organizations don’t plan to face these scenarios. Yet, the NFL had seen this before. In November 1963, only 48 hours after the assassination of President Kennedy, the NFL, after some back-and-forth debate, decided that they should play their scheduled games to show that life could go on and offer a distraction from the shock of that event in Dallas. They even received encouragement from White House officials. What transpired was some of the most uninspired football seen to date. The players’ hearts and minds were not in the game, with several players saying they were just going through the motions. That carried over to fan reaction. Between the backlash for playing so soon in the wake of a national tragedy and the blowback from the poor caliber of play, many of the league’s powerbrokers felt they made a bad mistake and if given a mulligan, they would make a different choice. Nearly 48 years later, the NFL faced a similar dilemma. This time, the league decided to postpone the games, announcing the final decision Wednesday, Sept 12 and flexing the originally scheduled Week 2 games to the end of the season. This extended the league season by one week, ultimately moving the Super Bowl, the crowning pop culture event of January, into February for the first time. When the league returned to play, there was increased security across the board as well as outpourings of American patriotism. One of the games that weekend would be the New York Jets, still reeling from what they saw on Sept 11, flying up to New England to play the Patriots. The game started with a tribute to the first responders, especially as Patriots lineman Joe Andruzzi walked out with his three FDNY brothers, and ended with Patriots’ starter Drew Bledsoe injured in a losing effort, his place taken by Tom Brady. 9/11 did spur some significant changes to the league. Stadium security was ramped up. The NFL, once it crossed the Rubicon of playing the Super Bowl in February, made it a permanent move. In years past, to keep the game in January, the league might only have one week between the conference title game and the Super Bowl. Originally, the league planned to keep only a one-week gap between the conference championships and the Super Bowl for the 2001 and 2002 seasons, since they only switched to starting the weekend after Labor Day in 1999, and the 2001 and 2002 seasons’ Super Bowl locations and dates were already set. The league still kept the original date for the Super Bowl as the last Sunday in January 2003, but that would be the last time Super Sunday took place in January. It also ensured that the league would always get the two-week gap between conference titles and the Super Bowl. Patriotic displays, not always a common occurrence pre-9/11, save the playing of the national anthem, started to become a bigger part of the pregame ceremonies. Yet, even without the attacks on September 11th, 2001 was always going to be a season in transition. That season would be the last under the old NFL model. The league had 31 teams at that point, split into three divisions (East, West, Central). The AFC fielded 16 teams, one of which was the Seattle Seahawks, and the NFC fielded 15. The current four division construct would debut the following season, with all division consisting of 4 teams. To get the conferences to have the same number of teams (16), the expansion Houston Texans would take their place in the AFC, with the aforementioned Seahawks moving to the NFC. The playoff system would also change. For 2001, the three division winners and three wild cards would make the postseason in each conference, with the top two seeds gaining byes, and the Wild Card team with the best record getting a home playoff game for Wild Card Weekend. Under the four divisions, only division winners were assured of a home playoff game (top two division winners gained byes and only two wild cards). This held until 2021, when the league added a 7th playoff team in each conference, with only the #1 getting a first-round bye. Of course, the biggest change would be the addition of the 32nd team. On Sept 11th, the Houston Texans franchise had a head coach, a team name, a place that they would play in, knowledge that they would get the 1st pick in the upcoming draft…and not much else. If Los Angeles got their collective acts together to bring a franchise back to the second largest media market (the league had been out of the city for 6 years to that point), the Texans are never a franchise. Then again, had Bud Adams not nuked every bridge possible with the powerbrokers of Houston, the Oilers, and not the Titans, would have been faced with how to manage such a sudden disruption to the football schedule that second week of playing in 2001. This weekend, you will find no shortage of articles and podcasts discussing the impact of 9/11 and how it resonates today. It hit all facets of life in America, and the NFL was no exception. While not the most significant area of American life, 9/11 did leave its mark on the league. The respective tributes that…

title: 5 Bold Predictions for Ravens at Colts Regular Season Opener
summary: The Indianapolis Colts kick off their regular season at home against the Baltimore Ravens this afternoon, and here are five bold predictions ahead of today’s matchup: 1. Sauce Gardner locks down Zay Flowers earlyFlowers is dealing with a hamstring issue and drew a hefty target share expectation, but he’ll be seeing plenty of Sauce Gardner […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts scores a touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens during the first quarter at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2020 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Bobby Ellis/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts kick off their regular season at home against the Baltimore Ravens this afternoon, and here are five bold predictions ahead of today’s matchup: 1. Sauce Gardner locks down Zay Flowers early Flowers is dealing with a hamstring issue and drew a hefty target share expectation, but he’ll be seeing plenty of Sauce Gardner in man coverage. If Gardner wins that matchup in the first half, it takes away Baltimore’s easiest answer when the offensive line struggles — and that line is the year’s biggest question mark for the Ravens. 2. Colts RB Jonathan Taylor exploits Ravens head coach Jesse Minter’s defense again Taylor torched Minter’s Los Angeles Chargers defense for 94 total rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns last October, as head coach Jim Harbaugh’s former defensive coordinator. Minter’s scheme hasn’t fundamentally changed, and the Ravens are breaking in new pass rushers up front (with starting Pro Bowl defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike out). Expect Taylor to be the tone-setter often that keeps Indy’s offense ahead of schedule, especially with starting quarterback Daniel Jones working his way back from a torn Achilles early on. 3. The Colts win the pressure battle without blitzing much Minter’s defenses have historically blitzed at a low rate (19% last year), which means the Colts’ front — led by DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart — gets to win with four rushers against a Ravens line PFF ranks 24th in the league, including a center making his first career start. Clean pocket push, not exotic pressure packages, is how Indy and Colts veteran defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo gets to Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson. 4. Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones avoids the big mistake Jones enters surprisingly healthy after last year’s late Achilles injury, and Indy’s offense was historically explosive by EPA/play under Colts head coach Shane Steichen. If he protects the ball against a Baltimore defense that’s also breaking in new pieces, field position swings the Colts’ way in a game expected to be low-scoring and close. 5. Colts win a tight one at home, something like 24-20 Baltimore is favored by 3.5 with a 47.5 total , but a lot of that leans on unknowns — new OC Declan Doyle calling his first regular-season game, a shaky interior line, and Jackson playing behind a center with zero career starts. The Colts faithful’s rapid noise, plus a battle-tested Colts offensive identity tips a close one to Indianapolis.

title: Last chance to predict the Colts’ record this season.
summary: Everyone has an opinion, so here your chance to share yours on how you see the Colts’ season playing out. Betting lines are sitting between 7 and 8 wins for the Colts. If I had disposable income, I’d put an affordable amount on the over, but my optimistic view should come as no surprise. I […]
full_text: Everyone has an opinion, so here your chance to share yours on how you see the Colts’ season playing out. Betting lines are sitting between 7 and 8 wins for the Colts. If I had disposable income, I’d put an affordable amount on the over, but my optimistic view should come as no surprise. I think we are going to be good and yes, good enough to be playoff bound and the winner of what I think might end up being the best division in the AFC. By the best division, I predict that the top three teams in our division, will have more wins than any other AFC division’s top three teams. I’m going to go 12 – 5 for our record. A tough early season schedule gives us the opportunity to provide the confidence that we need to keep momentum throughout the regular season. If healthy, we will be among the teams with shorter odds to win it all, as the playoffs start. I’m going to trust my eyes from last year and believe that our offense will be the kind that gives everyone we play fits. I saw us run some better screen action during the preseason and I have to believe that it will be the answer to the answer that defenses found against us in the second half of last year. Of course, health has to go our way. I don’t think we are as “injury prone”, as some suggest. Some point to the CBs and are worried. The way I see it, Ward and Gardner got hurt last year and Ward was on and off of the IR multiple times, but neither are what I would call injury prone. Walley was hurt for the entire year, but it was one of one, so has he been around long enough to be prone? D. Jones has had some injuries, but those who point to missed games should also look at his designation on some of those weeks he missed as a Giant. He was their QB of the future and they sat him when it was a questionable choice. We also need our DTs to be out there consistently. No doubt we are better when Buck and Grove are out there. I like our depth everywhere else, at least in small doses. I also think that although Allen may not shine early, he will be that guy that is always involved and will be a stud by the time we are awaiting a post season opponent. My biggest fear is Shane. I love his ability to game plan, but I am less confident his adjustments and game management. If we lose because we are not prepared, or because we did not do well situationally, it will be on Shane. That will be the end of both he and Ballard. The AFC in general is not the gauntlet that it has been over the last five years. There is no reason why we cant be the new sheriff in town. Okay, there are reasons and I will acknowledge them when they appear, but at this early date, optimism is just as easy as angst, so full speed ahead! Thanks for your time and Go Colts!

title: Is Parker Washington Worth a Michael Wilson Contract?
summary: Per multiple reports, the Jacksonville Jaguars and wide receiver Parker Washington are “unlikely” to finalize a contract extension before the start of the 2026 regular season. Per NFL Network’s Cam Wolfe, the team reportedly presented Washington’s camp with an offer in the range of the three-year, $75 million deal Arizona Cardinals receiver Michael Wilson signed […]
full_text: Per multiple reports, the Jacksonville Jaguars and wide receiver Parker Washington are “unlikely” to finalize a contract extension before the start of the 2026 regular season. Per NFL Network’s Cam Wolfe, the team reportedly presented Washington’s camp with an offer in the range of the three-year, $75 million deal Arizona Cardinals receiver Michael Wilson signed last week, a deal worth $25 million per year and $47 million guaranteed. Washington’s camp, however, does not appear ready to sign at that number, and with the clock running down before Sunday’s opener against the Cleveland Browns, both sides seem set to let the negotiations carry into the regular season. The development is not entirely surprising. While ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported earlier this week that Washington would prefer not to let the talks linger into the regular season, recent reporting also indicates that that preference would not result in them accepting the seemingly fair (on the surface) contract offered by Jacksonville. Per Jordan Schultz: “Ultimately, sources say that Parker Washington and the Jaguars simply could not agree with the compensation on a new deal. Jacksonville has big plans for him in this year two offense under Liam Coen, and despite not agreeing to an extension, my understanding is that the relationship between both sides “remains in a healthy place.” Clearly Extension Worthy Washington, 24, was drafted by Jacksonville in the sixth round of the 2023 NFL Draft, with the 185th overall pick out of Penn State. At 5-foot-10 and 204 pounds, he entered the league as an undersized slot receiver with good hands and excellent route-running ability, and he has spent three years turning a sixth-round profile into a limited, albeit dominant first-team conversation. Career NFL Statistics (entering 2026), per Pro Football Reference: Receptions: 106 Receiving Yards: 1,369 Receiving Average: 12.9 Receiving Touchdowns: 10 Return Yards: 859 Return Touchdowns: 3 2025 Season Statistics, per PFF: Games Played: 16 (7 starts) Targets: 95 (team-leading) Receptions: 58 Receiving Yards: 847 Receiving Touchdowns: 5 Yards Per Reception: 14.6 Yards After Catch: 277 Drops: 6 Advanced Stats Average Depth of Target: 13.1 yards Yards Per Route Run: 2.06 (14th of all WRs with 400+ routes run) Yards Per Target: 8.9 (22nd) Explosive Plays: 18 (8th) PFF Overall Grade: 79.3 (18th among 81 qualified wide receivers) PFF Receiving Grade: 82.4 (14th among 81 qualified wide receivers) Those numbers represent a clear breakout by any reasonable measure. Washington led the team in targets, catches, and receiving yards while playing in fewer than half the game’s starting snaps. The production was spread evenly enough that the raw statistics do not fully capture his impact, and by the time the calendar turned to December, the national conversation around Washington had shifted meaningfully. 2025 Stretch Run The extension talks didn’t gain immediate urgency due to Washington’s full-season stat line. They gained urgency because of what he did over the final month of the regular season and into the postseason. Over his final four games, including the Wild Card matchup against the Buffalo Bills, Washington accumulated 454 receiving yards and three touchdowns. pic.twitter.com/eLtsb2CjuY — Performances (@NotPerformances) December 22, 2025 His Week 16 performance against the Denver Broncos was the headline moment, six receptions for a career-high 145 yards including a career-long 63-yard reception, and a touchdown. In the Wild Card loss to Buffalo, he totaled 109 yards including a 34-yard gain and a fourth-quarter touchdown that temporarily gave Jacksonville a four-point lead. That is the version of Washington that his camp believes is worth significantly more than $25 million per year. That is also, likely, the version of Washington that the Jaguars need to see sustained over a full season before they can fully commit to the number his camp is reportedly seeking. The Michael Wilson Comp The Jaguars’ offer is reportedly framed around the Wilson contract, and the comparison is somewhat a reasonable starting point, though it requires some scrutiny on both sides. Wilson’s deal was a three-year $75 million extension worth up to $78 million with $47 million guaranteed. Spotrac placed Wilson’s pre-signing market value at $18 million per year, meaning Arizona paid a moderate premium for the security of keeping him following his dominant play in limited stretches. Wilson finished 2025 with 78 receptions, 1,006 yards, and seven touchdowns, 159 more yards, two more touchdowns, and considerably more consistency across a full 17-game campaign than Washington’s 2025 line. There are meaningful differences in context, however. Wilson was a third-round pick who played three full seasons in Arizona’s offense. Washington is a sixth-round pick with one breakout year on his ledger, seven starts in 16 appearances, and a stretch-run performance that is genuinely elite, but that also came in part with Travis Hunter sidelined and the depth of Jacksonville’s receiver room temporarily reduced. The offer doesn’t seem unreasonable. Whether it is sufficient given what Washington’s camp believes he has already proven is a different question. Final Four Games (2025): 10 Targets: 6 Receptions for 145 yards and a TD 10 Targets: 8 Receptions for 115 yards 9 Targets: 5 Receptions for 87 yards and a TD 12 Targets: 7 Receptions for 107 yards and a TD (playoffs vs Bills) The Case For Extension Washington is 24 years old and entering what should be his statistical prime. His PFF receiving grade of 82.4 ranked 14th in the NFL last season. He led a Super Bowl-contending offense in targets and caught the ball in critical moments when the stakes were highest. His chemistry with Trevor Lawrence is among the strongest on the roster, and offensive coordinator Grant Udinski and head coach Liam Coen have both repeatedly singled him out as a key player in this scheme. Most Contested Catches by WRs ( @PFF ) 27- Puka Nacua 22- Michael Wilson 22- George Pickens 18- Jauan Jennings 18- Tee Higgins 18- Ja’Marr Chase 17- Parker Washington 17- Nico Collins 17- Courtland Sutton 17- AJ Brown — Daniel Griffis (@DanDGriffis) January 20, 2026 His value as a punt returner, with three career return touchdowns, also adds a dimension that virtually no comparable contract compensates for. At $25 to $30 million per year, Jacksonville locks in a player at the peak of his development arc before the market inevitably resets even higher. Receiver contracts only trend one direction, and losing Washington to free agency after a second breakout season in 2026 would cost significantly more than the deal currently on the table. The Case Against The counterargument against paying more than $25 million begins and ends with the proving period. Washington has one productive NFL season, and within that season, seven starts in sixteen appearances and six drops against a catch rate that checked in at 61 percent on 95 targets. His late-season surge was real, but it arrived in a context shaped by favorable circumstances: Travis Hunter’s absence expanded his target share The opponents softened toward the end of the schedule Brian Thomas Jr’s muted 2025 performance likely added more targets to Washington The Wilson comparison cuts both ways. Wilson reached 1,000 yards in a full season of work and has three seasons of consistent production behind him. Washington’s resume, as compelling as its trajectory seems, does not yet match the body of evidence Arizona used to justify a comparable number. If the Jaguars commit $75 million or more on one strong second half and a playoff game, and Washington’s 2026 production comes in closer to his full-season 2025 line than his closing stretch, that contract will draw scrutiny from every direction. A contract of that amount, with that sample size would seem to be above the market rate, while betting on promise, even more than the Wilson contract. The asking…

full_text: On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs are home under the lights at Arrowhead Stadium , taking on the Denver Broncos . Let’s see how the game plays out in Madden NFL 2 7. STOP! If you want to watch the simulation without spoilers, start this video — or if you can’t see it, click here. First quarter The Chiefs’ defense held strong on the Broncos’ opening drive as Denver went three-and-out. Chris Jones made it look easy, getting through the Broncos’ offensive line for a tackle for loss to help force the punt. The absence of Josh Simmons paid dividends as Nik Bonitto was able to sack Mahomes, forcing the Chiefs to punt. Kenneth Walker’s first carry in a Chiefs uniform went for two yards. End of first quarter: Broncos 0, Chiefs 0 Second quarter J.K. Dobbins was able to pick up a first down on the first play of the quarter, getting the Broncos inside the Chiefs’ 10-yard line. One play later, Bo Nix connected with Troy Franklin on a hard flat route for a nine-yard touchdown to give the Broncos the lead. Brashard Smith picked up 21 yards on a second-down run, putting the Chiefs inside Broncos territory for the first time of the game at the Broncos’ 38-yard line. Three plays later, the Chiefs faced a third-and-eight, and Broncos defensive tackle D.J. Jones sacked Mahomes, pushing the Chiefs outside of field-goal range and forcing them to punt on a promising drive. Following the Chiefs’ punt, Nix threw three straight incompletions before Denver punted the ball back to Kansas City. Bonitto sacked Mahomes for the second time of the game on third-and-six in Broncos territory, once again pushing the Chiefs out of field-goal range. The battle of field position continued. The Broncos would punt it back to the Chiefs, and on the ensuing drive, Mahomes dotted up Xavier Worthy twice. The first reception got the Chiefs across midfield, while another with 16 seconds left got them to the Broncos’ 25-yard line. Mahomes would end up being sacked by Zach Allen as time ran out in the half. End of second quarter: Broncos 7, Chiefs 0 Third quarter Andy Reid dialed up more chances for Mahomes to throw the football, as two first-down passes to Worthy and one to Tyquan Thornton helped the Chiefs get across midfield. Then it was the Kenneth Walker show, as he ripped off a 15-yard run before breaking loose for a 29-yard touchdown to tie the game. Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s name was called in the rotation, and he made the most of it, sacking Nix to force the Broncos to punt on their opening drive of the second half. The Chiefs went three-and-out. The Broncos went three-and-out. On third-and-six from the Chiefs’ own 46-yard line, Mahomes rifled a pass down the middle of the field to Thornton, who took it to the 22-yard line. One play later, a handoff to Walker got the Chiefs to the one-yard line. End of third quarter: Broncos 7, Chiefs 7 Fourth quarter On second-and-goal, Mahomes found his favorite target, Travis Kelce, for the touchdown to give the Chiefs the lead. The Broncos punted back to the Chiefs. The Chiefs once again punted back to the Broncos. The Broncos punted. Mahomes was sacked for the fifth time of the game on third down, forcing the Chiefs to punt. Nix, from the Broncos’ own 46-yard line, found a streaking Evan Engram, who somehow burned three Chiefs defenders before dropping a catch in the end zone. End of the fourth quarter: Broncos 14, Chiefs 14 Overtime The Chiefs’ defense forced the Broncos’ offense to go three-and-out and punt the ball back to Kansas City. The Chiefs marched downfield, and the Mahomes-to-Worthy connection resulted in two first downs. Walker rushed to the Broncos ‘ 12-yard line. Tyquan Thornton was left wide open in the end zone, and Mahomes found him on a post route for the game-winning touchdown. Final score: Chiefs 20, Broncos 14 Notable stats Patrick Mahomes: 18 for 23, 204 passing yards, 2 touchdowns Box Nix: 15 for 25, 157 passing yards, 2 touchdowns Kenneth Walker: 15 rushing attempts, 102 rushing yards, 1 touchdown J.K Dobbins: 11 rushing attempts, 24 rushing yards R.J. Harvey: 5 rushing attempts, 6 rushing yards. Xavier Worthy: 7 receptions, 105 yards Tyquan Thornton: 4 receptions, 70 yards Travis Kelce: 3 receptions, 20 yards, 1 touchdown Troy Franklin: 5 receptions, 65 yards, 1 touchdown Evan Engram: 4 receptions, 44 yards Courtland Sutton: 2 receptions, 13 yards Nik Bonitto: 3 sacks, 4 tackles for loss Zach Allen: 2 sacks, 3 tackles for loss Felix Anduike-Uzomah: 1 sack Chris Jones: 6 tackles, 2 tackles for loss Next week, will once again be under the lights, but this time for Sunday Night Football vs. the Indianapolis Colts . title: Should the Chiefs be open to a major in-season trade?
summary: Earlier this week, the Arrowhead Pride staff shared five bold predictions before the season begins. Jared Sapp wrote a sixth that rookie site manager Ron Kopp Jr. overlooked when gathering responses: the Chiefs will execute a major in-season trade for an offensive weapon. He’s no longer held to the “prediction” because of the exclusion, but […]
full_text: Aug 15, 2026; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs general manager Brett Veach enters the stadium prior to the pre season game against the Los Angeles Rams at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Earlier this week, the Arrowhead Pride staff shared five bold predictions before the season begins. Jared Sapp wrote a sixth that rookie site manager Ron Kopp Jr. overlooked when gathering responses: the Chiefs will execute a major in-season trade for an offensive weapon. He’s no longer held to the “prediction” because of the exclusion, but fortunately for us, Jared decided to elaborate further on the question: Should the Chiefs be open to a major in-season trade? The Kansas City Chiefs have repeatedly shown the ability to overhaul the defense in an offseason. The 2026 season will mark the third major defensive overhaul since coordinator Steve Spagnuoulo joined the Chiefs in 2019. The team has been much more hesitant in general, however, to tinker with the offense. That won’t be an option going forward. Tight end Travis Kelce is almost certainly in his final season. Dependability (on multiple fronts) continues to be too much of a concern for pending free agent wide receiver Wide receiver Rashee Rice to justify a lucrative long-term extension. 2024 first round selection Xavier Worthy’s lack of size appears to limit his ceiling as a starting wideout. At every opportunity through the trade deadline, general manager Brett Veach needs to have his eyes on what the offense is going to look like in 2027 and beyond. While the upcoming draft is deep at wide receiver, Veach has generally shown a preference for addressing needs ahead of time. Since starting wide receivers generally do not actually hit free agency, targeting an acquisition who would be amicable to a new contract in Kansas City ahead of the trade deadline would be a sound strategy. There are multiple ways this could go. One path could be a member of the 2024 draft class just becoming extension eligible. Multiple such players now play for coaching staffs that had no part in drafting them. Every year, there is also at least one veteran on a disappointing squad seeking a change of scenery. The Chiefs should be ready to pounce. Would the cost be high? Almost certainly. Kansas City is already up against the 2027 salary cap — mostly due to the contract adjustment for quarterback Patrick Mahomes that will assuredly be restructured in the spring. The Chiefs have an extra third round pick and may receive a fourth-round compensatory selection. Draft compensation in trades is always painful, but Veach has to consider any option before him. As Kansas City’s general manager, we have seen Veach twice trade first round selections for positions he could not address in free agency. The price paid to acquire defensive end Frank Clark in 2019 and left tackle Orlando Brown Jr. in 2021 can be debated, but both moves yielded starters on Super Bowl winning squads. If a chance is there before the early November trade deadline to add a cost controlled offensive weapon, Veach should be open to it.

We challenged each other, and overall it’s going to do good for us as a team.” Chiefs add Chris Jones to injury report before Monday night matchup with Broncos | A to Z Sports The news is less than ideal for Kansas City, especially considering that the Broncos boast what is widely considered one of the best offensive lines in football, led by left tackle Garrett Bolles and right guard Quinn Meinerz. After practicing Thursday and Friday, the Chiefs are scheduled to hold one final practice on Saturday, with a brief media look scheduled for 11:45 a.m. Central Time. That will be followed by head coach Andy Reid’s final address at 1 p.m. If Jones is limited or out, Chiefs rookie first-rounder Peter Woods would likely see more playing time. Chiefs Recognize Technical Sergeant Kenyan Francis as This Week’s Tribute to the Troops Honoree An Air Traffic Controller, Technical Sergeant Francis is tasked with ensuring the safe and efficient flow of both military and civilian aircraft while also training numerous other controllers to handle this critical role. It’s an invaluable responsibility, and when asked why he decided to join our Armed Forces 12 years ago, Francis didn’t mince words. “Everything I have done has been in the service of our country,” Francis said. “It has come with its sacrifices, but I wouldn’t change anything. I am grateful to the Air Force for giving me a great life trajectory. It has set me up to be successful in all aspects of my life.” NFL Week 1 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN What we’re hearing on the Chiefs: The biggest storyline for Monday’s game is the return of Mahomes. But Mahomes will need plenty of help to defeat the AFC West rival. WR Rashee Rice knows as much, especially since he’s entering the final season of his rookie contract as the Chiefs’ projected No. 1 receiving target. Rice wants to have a breakout season, and he was able to get through the Chiefs’ grueling training camp after having a surgery on his right knee in May. “Truthfully speaking, I think I’m more in shape than I was [last season],” Rice said Thursday. “I’m more confident in being in the spots that I have to be, as far as being on the same page as [Mahomes] because we’re both coming off an injury. We’re kind of seeing ourselves get back to our full potential.” — Nate Taylor Around the NFL Report: Bears, D’Andre Swift agree to a three-year, $33.75 milion extension that includes $27.5 million guaranteed | NFL.com “I always look inside-out,” McVay said. “I didn’t do a good enough job getting us ready to go. There were some opportunities where maybe the game could have flipped, but they deserved the win. They were ready to go. And we’ll look at it. We’ll see where we can improve and be better moving forward. “But this is a good humbling day. This is what can sometimes happen in sports. I love this locker room and, you know, the first thing that I’m going to look at is myself, and I have to do a better job for a group collectively, with our coaches, with our players, and we’ll look at this film, and we’ll get back to work because, clearly, that’s obviously what we’ve got to do, and sometimes sports can humble you, and today was one of those days.” Sources: 49ers reward Kyle Shanahan with multiyear extension | ESPN The San Francisco 49ers have given a multiyear extension to coach Kyle Shanahan, sources confirmed to ESPN on Friday. Terms of the deal, which was first reported by The Ringer, are not yet known, but he had been under contract with San Francisco through the 2027 season. In his 10 seasons, Shanahan has an 83-67 regular-season record and has guided the 49ers to six playoff appearances, including Super Bowls trips — both losses — following the 2019 and 2023 seasons. He has won 10 or more games in a season five times. Falcons to start Cooper Rush at QB with Tua Tagovailoa ruled out | The Athletic Rush was named the starting quarterback Friday afternoon after Tagovailoa was ruled out for the game because of an oblique injury suffered in Thursday’s practice. Penix, who is still rehabbing a torn ACL suffered in Week 11 last year, has also been ruled out, meaning Jack Strand, the undrafted rookie out of Division II Minnesota State-Moorhead, will be Rush’s backup. “The mindset and prep hasn’t changed,” Strand said. “That’s how it has to be for any QB in the room. … Always in the back of your head, you have to be ready to go.” In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride The Chiefs’ 2026 season, starting Week 1, is all on Andy Reid This season is about a lot of things, but really it’s about one thing: Is Andy Reid still the elite coach he’s been for the better part of the last 25 years? If he is, the Chiefs should be just fine in his steady hands. If he’s not, we might look back at this week’s offensive line decisions as the first indication of what’s to come. All eyes will be focused on the left side of the line Monday night, but the spotlight is still on Reid. title: Rams suggested as landing spot for reunion with former tackle
summary: The Washington Commanders released tackle D.J. Humphries on Friday, opening the door for him to return to the Los Angeles Rams as insurance for A.J. Jackson if that’s something both parties are interested in. Humphries appeared in eight games with the Rams in 2025, including one start in place of Jackson. It is also possible […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 12: D.J. Humphries #72 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 12, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Washington Commanders released tackle D.J. Humphries on Friday, opening the door for him to return to the Los Angeles Rams as insurance for A.J. Jackson if that’s something both parties are interested in. Humphries appeared in eight games with the Rams in 2025, including one start in place of Jackson. It is also possible that the Commanders are simply releasing Humphries for roster considerations with the expectation to re-sign him in Week 2, but in any case the Rams do have the opportunity to sign the veteran tackle if they want. This is interesting – the Commanders just released veteran tackle DJ Humphries . Im curious what the corresponding move will be pic.twitter.com/BpGGKclHDV — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) September 11, 2026 Josh Buckhalter of Heavy suggested the Rams should reach out to Humphries in case Jackson is suspended or loses time due to injury again: Humphries also has one start in four postseason appearances and has a pre-existing relationship with Rams assistant head coach Kliff Kingsbury. “The offense is kind of–it’s kind of the offense that I ran earlier with Kliff and, I guess, a lot of that same stuff,” Humphries told reporters in August, underscoring how much of an impact the first-year Rams coach had on him (and the Commanders). “It’s easier for me to kind of mesh in. “ Humphries was the 24th overall pick in the 2015 draft by the Arizona Cardinals. He started 98 games with the Cardinals over eight seasons and has since signed with the Chiefs, Rams, and Commanders. He has been firmly entrenched as a backup over the past two years. Possible D.J. Humphries consideration (beyond a flat-out release): * Vested veterans (4+ years) have their contracts guaranteed for the season if on the Week 1 roster. * Therefore, someone from the PS is elevated for Week 1 as OL8, or they keep Wylie, Gulbin, Togiai active *… — Ben Standig (@BenStandig) September 11, 2026 Jackson has not been suspended by the NFL yet and may not be suspended at all. However, L.A. only has one backup left tackle right now and it’s 36-year-old journeyman David Quessenberry. With Humphries now a free agent again, perhaps Les Snead would feel more comfortable with him coming back to the Rams.

title: Jaylen Watson on wrong end of 2 TD passes in Rams debut
summary: Rams cornerback Jaylen Watson was only blamed for one touchdown pass surrendered in his last two seasons with the Chiefs, but L.A.’s $51 million investment has already allowed twice that many in 2026. Although “blame” on touchdown passes can be difficult to ascertain, especially if it’s simply because Watson was the closest defender in the […]
full_text: Rams cornerback Jaylen Watson was only blamed for one touchdown pass surrendered in his last two seasons with the Chiefs, but L.A.’s $51 million investment has already allowed twice that many in 2026. Although “blame” on touchdown passes can be difficult to ascertain, especially if it’s simply because Watson was the closest defender in the area, this is not the start that the Rams envisioned for him when they overhauled their secondary in the offseason. In total, Watson was blamed for allowing three catches on five targets, resulting in 53 yards and two touchdowns. On the first touchdown, Watson is covering Mike Evans on the bottom of the screen and then has to run all the way down the field to try and cover Demarcus Robinson as he has sprinted past and away from safety Kam Kinchens. This is where one touchdown and the majority of the yards against Watson come from. PURDY GOES DEEP FOR THE TOUCHDOWN!!! SFvsLAR on Netflix pic.twitter.com/SCggzxjqLo — NFL (@NFL) September 11, 2026 This is a better visual of how far Watson had to run just to be in the area: Jaylen Watson hauling so much ass trying to get there pic.twitter.com/wG9YGU0Dry https://t.co/VC37NI9nG6 — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) September 11, 2026 Watson, who ended up with a toe injury just before the flight to Australia, was just too slow to get there. 7 step drops under center with no play action, what year is it? Beauty of a ball by Purdy, on a play where I think Jaylen Watson plays this out just a step too slow (not having 95 in the game helps too) pic.twitter.com/wz8pJy1s30 — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) September 11, 2026 Of course, Watson is not a burner and that’s why he was a seventh round pick in 2022. It’s impressive that he’s built such a good NFL resume since then without speed. On the second touchdown, Watson is covering Evans at the goal line and gets dominated at the point of the catch. Mike Evans is so special, he MOSSED Jaylen Watson 🫣 pic.twitter.com/wh71yXugAj — Zane Hancock (@Zane_Hancock21) September 11, 2026 Evans might be a Hall of Fame receiver, but he won’t be the last tall red zone threat who Watson has to cover in the end zone this season. Next week, the Rams are facing the Giants with Malik Nabers (if he’s active) and Odell Beckham, Jr.. Last season, Watson was only blamed for allowing one touchdown and that came in his final game with the Chiefs against the Titans in Week 16. However, it did seem like quarterbacks were getting more comfortable with attacking Watson as the season wore on, including seven catches for 104 yards allowed against the Cowboys in Week 13. Watson only appeared in six games in 2024 and didn’t allow any touchdowns. Watson’s debut with the Rams was not ideal, just as it wasn’t a great day for Myles Garrett or Matthew Stafford or Davante Adams. It wasn’t much of a day for anyone on the Rams. He’ll have his chance to rebound next Sunday and with the money that L.A. spent to upgrade the cornerbacks from last season, he’s going to need to.

title: Myles Garrett, Rams, may have a knee problem
summary: Myles Garrett did not get off to the start that he wanted to in Week 1 against the San Francisco 49ers, and though there were/are some positive signs, Garrett stating after the game that more or less he wasn’t himself due to injury, should be concerning. Even if only in the short-term. Garrett can put […]
full_text: MELBOURNE, AUSTRALIA - SEPTEMBER 11: Myles Garrett #95 of the Los Angeles Rams warms up prior to the NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on September 11, 2026 in Melbourne, Australia. (Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) | Getty Images Myles Garrett did not get off to the start that he wanted to in Week 1 against the San Francisco 49ers, and though there were/are some positive signs , Garrett stating after the game that more or less he wasn’t himself due to injury, should be concerning. Even if only in the short-term. Garrett can put all this worry to rest with a strong game against the New York Giants in Week 2 , but until then, what we have to go off of is that Garrett and the entire team had a disappointing Week 1, and that Garrett said he didn’t feel great during the game. It’s something to monitor. What else is there to monitor? The Sunday games. Football is back. NFC West: Myles Garrett acknowledges knee injury is significant after quiet Rams debut (sports.mynorthwest) “This was the worst version of myself that I’ve put out there, and I’ve got to be better,” Garrett said at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. “I’ve got to find a way to recover and get back to the player I know I can be and I’ve shown that I’ve been before.” Garrett didn’t want to discuss details of his knee or his overall health after finishing without a tackle for only the fourth time in 135 career NFL games. He wouldn’t even say which knee is injured. “I wasn’t the player that I wanted to be, and I feel like I wasn’t the player I’ve been before when I’ve stepped onto that field,” Garrett said. “I’ve got to do what I can to get back to that.” Myles Garrett’s comments, usage are concerning (nbcsports.com) ““When I was out there I was a little more focused on myself and trying to stay healthy than what they were doing, and it showed,” Garrett said. That’s alarming. And unusual. Typically, players don’t play if concerns about their health become a distraction to the task at hand. It’s fair to wonder why Garrett played — and why the Rams didn’t intervene and stop him from playing. It’s also fair to wonder whether the Rams knew about Garrett’s circumstances. If they had, the Rams may not have used him for six special-teams snaps, hopeful he’d show off his ability to block a kick, or two.“ ‘What Did He Do All Offseason’ — NFL Analyst Unleashes on Myles Garrett After Disappointing Rams Debut (sports.yahoo) “The Rams traded for Garrett from the Cleveland Browns . Garrett’s debut performance caught the attention of ESPN Cleveland analyst Tony Rizzo, who questioned how the reigning Defensive Player of the Year had prepared for the season and said: “What did he do all offseason? Went to this thing, went to that thing, was in LA doing commercials, and you show up like that in Game 1 after the team gave up everything for you? Bad look, man. Bad look. Karma is a (expletive), isn’t it?” 3 overreactions to Rams’ disappointing loss to 49ers in Week 1 (nflspinzone.com) “Even though Donald didn’t play in this game as he ramps back up to game speed, The Rams getting smacked around like they did (27-7) was rather jaw-dropping. And we have a handful of overreactions to the game that we have to talk through. 3 overreactions to Rams’ ugly loss to 49ers in Week 1 1. The Rams overpaid (badly) for Myles Garrett The Rams obviously traded a king’s ransom to the Cleveland Browns this offseason to get Myles Garrett in a trade. Coming off of a truly historic season, their investment was justified. Garrett racked up an NFL-record 23 sacks last season, along with 33 tackles for loss. The Rams acquiring him has felt all offseason like an unfair advantage, but the 49ers were able to neutralize him rather easily.“ Betting buzz: Rams suffer worst opening loss by preseason Super Bowl favorite in 50 years “The Rams lost 27-7 to the San Francisco 49ers , becoming the first preseason Super Bowl favorite to lose its opener by 20 or more in the past 50 seasons, according to SportsOddHistory.com. The 1993 Dallas Cowboys lost by 19, and the 2017 New England Patriots and 1987 New York Giants each lost by 15 in their season openers. Both the Cowboys and Patriots would play in the Super Bowl in those seasons, with the Cowboys winning and the Patriots losing, but the Giants failed to make the playoffs.“ Los Angeles Rams ‘Terminated’ Deal With 6-Foot-1 Ball-Hawking Cornerback (sports.yahoo) “The decision–which Rams On SI’s Blaine Grisak reported on September 10–was actually the culmination of a multi-day process in which the Rams ultimately severed ties with Johnson. Rams Finalize Process to Cut Ties With Alex Johnson According to the NFL’s transaction wire, the Rams “terminated” Johnson’s deal “via waivers” on September 10, but they agreed to an injury settlement with the former Bruin on September 9. The Rams officially waived Johnson with an injury designation on August 29, announcing it as part of their deadline cuts. Johnson cleared waivers and reverted back to the Rams’ injured reserve.“ LA Rams’ Offensive Split Exposes Clear Problem After 49ers Loss (heavy.com) “ Sports Illustrated ‘s Blaine Grisak highlighted a striking personnel split from Los Angeles’ 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers on Sept. 10. According to Grisak, the Rams averaged 0.21 expected points added per play on 21 snaps from 13 personnel — one running back, three tight ends and one receiver. On 32 plays from 11 personnel, which puts three receivers on the field, they averaged minus-0.66 EPA per play.“ 49ers-Rams: Exposing some bad takes made before the game (ninersnation) “Now don’t get too excited. This was Week 1. I’m the first to tell you never to take stock in Week 1 games because it’s almost a given that teams look sloppy and have rust to knock off. The thing is, the 49ers looked really good. Not sloppy-play, good, but just good. Sure, it’s Week 1, and the 49ers could come back to earth next week, but it’s the Rams, and I can’t help myself. So let’s be petty and make fun of some bad takes made before the game while we have time! Bill Plaschke: “Rams will go undefeated on their way to winning another home Super Bowl title ” We had a couple of those “Rams are running the table” takes going around, but none got more notorious than the Los Angeles Times’ Bill Plaschke and his column on how the Rams are going to go 17-0. I’m going to make a crazy take myself: I don’t think the Rams are running the table.“ NFL Week 1 picks: Upset and score predictions, matchup breakdowns for every game (nfl.com) “My pick is largely tied to belief in Johnson’s offense and my continued skepticism about a Bryce Young -led attack being able to score enough to consistently win. Yes, there’s been a lot of hand-wringing about whether the Bears truly have upgraded their defense, which allowed the fourth-most yards in the league last season and made taking the ball away its signature — a risky way of doing business from year to year. I’m not sure the Panthers are prepared to fully take advantage of Chicago’s weakness, with questions of their own at offensive tackle. Now, Carolina spent big on defense this offseason with the signings of LB Devin Lloyd and OLB Jaelan Phillips . If Ejiro Evero’s crew comes out guns blazing and never lets Williams settle in, things could easily swing in the home team’s favor. Unfortunately, the Panthers will be without the player who was supposed to be Phillips’ top running mate off the edge, as Carolina’s sacks co-leader from last season, Nic Scourton , is out for the season with an ACL tear.“ Comment of the Day: “There are many reasons we lost last night but one thing stands out to me and I want to focus on that specific thing. McVay’s pass play calling has been poor ever since we won the super bowl. We win in spite of his play calling, not because of it. Every since the super bowl win, he assumes he can have Stafford drop straight back, survey the field, and zip a perfect pass to a receiver for the…
author: Danny Stone

title: Week 1 always lies. These parts of the Rams’ loss might not.
summary: Week 1 of the NFL season is certain to bring unexpected outcomes. For instance, the Seattle Seahawks fell short to the San Francisco 49ers in Sam Darnold’s first game last year before going on to win the Super Bowl. The New England Patriots, who also made the final two, suffered a loss in the opening […]
full_text: MELBOURNE, AUSTRALIA - SEPTEMBER 11: Myles Garrett #95 of the Los Angeles Rams warms up prior to the NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on September 11, 2026 in Melbourne, Australia. (Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 1 of the NFL season is certain to bring unexpected outcomes. For instance, the Seattle Seahawks fell short to the San Francisco 49ers in Sam Darnold’s first game last year before going on to win the Super Bowl. The New England Patriots, who also made the final two, suffered a loss in the opening week to the Las Vegas Raiders. Our job today is to analyze which parts of the Los Angeles Rams’ stunning loss to the 49ers could be sustainable and which may be fake. We only have real information from a single game. The only certainty in the NFL is change. To an extent, we cannot rely on past seasons to predict outcomes in 2026. Some of the Rams’ shortcomings are probably very real. Some may be isolated to a game that required heavy travel and a unique schedule in addition to a division rival that knows them well and is always more competitive than expected. The below areas are what I find to be most concerning in order to least concerning: #1 – Quarterback play & Stafford’s limitations It’s clear based on the reaction to this post that most Rams fans expect Matthew Stafford to bounce back after one of his worst games over his LA tenure. But what if he doesn’t? Quarterbacks can decline quickly and fall off a cliff. This is THE most important position in football. Everything starts and ends with the quarterback. The Rams only have a “super team” if their signal caller plays at a high level. It was always likely that Stafford would regress some from his MVP heights, largely because he reached that level for the first time after nearly 20 years in the NFL and because it is nearly impossible to repeat. No one was expecting regression to the extent we saw on Thursday night. Stafford looked old. He was more immobile than we had ever seen from him. He held the ball longer, invited pressure, and passed up what the defense was giving him. As we saw on Wednesday night with Drake Maye, defenses this season will require opposing quarterbacks to be patient and take the underneath throw. It takes discipline and commitment to sustain that plan for 60 minutes. Neither Stafford nor Maye showed they were able to do that through one game. We know Stafford isn’t mobile. Using his legs to mitigate pressure is not a realistic outcome. The tool he does have to minimize pressure is his mind and getting rid of the ball quickly—even if it means settling for shorter passes and going for the big play later. Here’s proof of why the over-aggression was ill-fated and how Stafford can get back on track next time. Data from Pro Football Focus (PFF). On throws aimed 20+ yards down field: 0/3 with an interception/TWP 10-19 yards: 3/7 (42.9%) for 74 yards and a TWP* 0-9 yards: 10/12 (83.3%) for 63 yards and no turnover-worthy plays (TWP) Behind LOS: 2/2 (100%) for 18 yards *(includes a 41-yard catch by Puka Nacua that was mostly YAC) If there is a silver lining it’s that Stafford was still accurate in the short area of the field. However, this is not how Sean McVay and Stafford want to live. They don’t want to be hyper efficient. They prefer going for the kill shot and finding explosives through the air. Can they course correct? #2 – Myles Garrett’s knee Myles Garrett played 40 snaps, which comprised 62% of the total 65 defensive plays. That is not his normal workload and the broadcast suggested he looked gassed after missing recent practices with a knee injury. LA has maintained that Garrett’s knee issue and absence from practices have mostly been a matter of veteran treatment and keeping him ready for the season. It’s also true that Garrett was brought in for playoff success. Not Week 1. But the Rams traded Jared Verse and a treasure chest of draft capital for the star pass rusher. In order to reap the benefits of the trade he needs to be on the field. I would expect his snap count to increase over time, although I can’t shake the feeling that there’s more to this knee injury than the team is letting on. We also cannot ignore the fact that Garrett was primarily aligned with the best left tackle in football: Trent Williams. While Garrett has gotten the better of Williams in the past, a limited offensive scheme (we will get to that later) also took away opportunities for Garrett to affect the game. I’m more worried about Garrett than I was last week. The concern isn’t regarding performance but more availability. It’s something we will need to track over the coming weeks. #3 – Staying on schedule offensively & 13 personnel The 49ers had great success on first down, which put LA behind the chains and setup less favorable looks on second and third down. LA converted just two of nine third downs against the 49ers. That won’t get the job done. But the bigger problem is that trailing on the scoreboard and being behind the chains limits LA’s approach from a personnel standpoint. The 13 personnel wrinkle has brought a significant advantage to LA; however, it offers little upside on second and third and long or when you need to mount a comeback. The Rams were significantly less effective in 11 personnel than when they had three tight ends on the field. This graphic is from SumerSports. Game script forced the Rams into 11 personnel on 56.1% of plays. They were in 12 personnel 7% of the time and spent 36.8% of their plays in 13. This played right into San Francisco’s hand. The lack of effectiveness with three receivers and a single tight end may underscore LA’s need for a third receiver and the idea that Davante Adams could take a step back from 2025. This was a looming concern in the offseason, although LA did not make a high-profile receiver addition. Do they have enough firepower if they aren’t playing with a lead? #4 – Jaylen Watson’s debut The Rams brought in Jaylen Watson in order to add much-needed size to the corner room and limit bigger receivers. Mike Evans got the best of him on an end zone fade. That cannot happen. Trent McDuffie immediately proved his value but defending multiple passes in the first quarter and stuffing an early screen play. Watson’s impact was less visible, although this wasn’t a disaster of a game. The outcome still fell below expectations. He needs to perform better in the upcoming games. #5 – Scheming around LA’s pass rushers & lack of pressure In comparison to the numbers outlined for Stafford above, 82.4% of Brock Purdy’s passes came within nine yards of the line of scrimmage. 12 attempts (35.3%) were behind the line. Purdy was not asked to win this game. He was mostly playing point guard. It worked to great effect. Most offenses won’t be able to sustain production against the Rams’ defense. The 49ers’ have strong scheme and YAC players that are uniquely equipped to run such a limited offensive game plan. I feel this is one of the least sustainable parts of the Rams’ loss, although similar outcomes could re-occur in the second game against San Francisco or versus teams like the Seahawks. #6 – Ending up in the losing column Being a historical betting favorite to win the Super Bowl doesn’t guarantee you a championship. It does, however, suggest that the floor is very high. The Rams will likely make the playoffs and earn a berth in the tournament. Whatever happens from that point is up to them. Dropping a game to a division rival is unfortunate. It doesn’t matter much in the grand scheme of things. LA can still take the second contest against San Francisco which will help in tie breakers. The season is far from over after the first game.

title: College football game day thread
summary: After a couple of weeks baking cupcakes, FBS football gets a little meat on the bone, matchup wise. The biggest play of the weekend is the battle between #1 Ohio State and #4 Texas, pitting two top QB/WR pairings. Julian Sayin and Jeremiah Smith for the Buckeyes versus Arch Manning and Cam Coleman for the […]
full_text: Jeremiah Smith #4 of the Ohio State Buckeyes is a favorite to be the #1 NFL draft selection in 2027(Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a couple of weeks baking cupcakes, FBS football gets a little meat on the bone, matchup wise. The biggest play of the weekend is the battle between #1 Ohio State and #4 Texas, pitting two top QB/WR pairings. Julian Sayin and Jeremiah Smith for the Buckeyes versus Arch Manning and Cam Coleman for the Longhorns. These are the 10 games TST will be monitoring, but feel free to weigh in on any game or prospects that strike your fancy. #6 Oregon @ Oklahoma St. 9 am on ESPN/Disney+ Eyes on: Oregon has Round 1 prospects QB Dante Moore, TE Jamari Johnson and DT A’Mauri Washington. Another DT, Bear Alexander, could get there by season’s end.Okie state has new coach and wide open offense that smothered in a Week 1 loss. Qb Drew Mestemaker, RB Caleb Hawkins and Wr Wyatt Young drive the attack. Arizona St. @ #10 Texas A&M 9 am on ABC Eyes on: The Sun Devils have re-loaded behind QB Cutter Boley, a deep RB rotation, and possible Round 1 WR Omarion Miller. WR Reed Harris is also a fine prospect. Texas A&M has an explosive offense helmed by run/throw threat Marcel Reed and speedster WR’s Mario Craver and Isaiah Horton. TJ Searcy and Anto Saka lead the defense. #11 Oklahoma @ Michigan 9 am on FOX Eyes on: Sooners QB John Mateer is back for his senior season and so is WR Isaiah Sategna, a threat with the ball in his hands. The aggressive defense is triggered by DT David Stone, E Taylor Wein, LB Owen Heinecke, and S Peyton Bowen. Michigan has a QB controversy, but RB Jordan Marshall can tote the rock. The OL is young, while the defense has a handful of Utah transfers to shoulder the load. #12 Alabama @ Kentucky 12:30 pm on ABC/Disney+ Eyes on: ‘ Bama is casting it’s lot with dual threat sophomore QB Keelon Russell behind a new and young OL. Ryan Coleman-Williams can have the drops, but is a gifted route runner and dangerous after the catch. Defensively, CB Zabien Brown and S Keon Sabb patrol the secondary and E Yahonzae Pierre can get after opposing QB’s. Kentucky has QB Kenny Minchey leading a revamped offense, throwing to top TE Willie Rodriguez. RB’s Jason Patterson and CJ Baxter are a one-two punch. Arizona @ #15 BYU 12:30 pm on FOX Eyes on: Arizona’s diminutive QB Noah Fifita is 5th year senior who has already thrown for 9000+yards. Giovanni Richardson and Tre Spivey are top targets. Kedrick Reescano is at the top of the RB rotation. BYU is led by sophomore QB Bear Bachmeier, his main target is true freshman WR Legend Glasker, while RB LJ Martin gets high draft grades. Mississippi St. @ Minnesota 1 2:30 on CBS Eyes on: Sophomore QB Kamario Taylor pulls the trigger for the Bulldogs. WR Anthony Evans is a threat after the catch and on returns. True freshman RB JJ Hill is big and fast. DE Will Whitson and S Issac Smith lead the defense. Minnesota QB Drake Lindsay is getting run as a top draft prospect. RB Darius Taylor is a threat running and receiving. Kerry Brown and John Nestor ate draft candidates in the secondary. #18 Tennessee @ Georgia Tech 4 pm on ESPN Eyes on: Dual threat true freshman QB Faizon Brandon runs the Tennessee attack, Desean Bishop provides thump in the run game, while WR’s Mike Mathews and Braylen Staley are playmakers. Georgia Tech runs behind RB’s Justice Haynes and Malachi Hosley, while jitterbug Jordan Allen is a threat receiving and on returns. LB EJ Lightsey is their defensive stud. #1 Ohio State @ #4 Texas 4:30 pm on ABC Eyes on: More than a battle between QB’s Arch Manning and Julian Sayin. The Buckeyes have likely #1 overall WR Jeremiah Smith and Texas counters with two stellar receivers of their own, Cam Coleman and Ryan Wingo. On defense, Ohio State matches top E Kenyatta Jackson against E Collin Simmons of Texas. Iowa St. @ #20 Iowa 4:30 pm on NBC Eyes on: Iowa State rebuilds with new coaches. Senior QB Jaylen Raynor was a standout at Arkansas State. WR’s Dominic Overby and Omari Hayes are his top targets. Walk-on Aiden Flora is RB#1. Iowa is again powered by their offensive line, with Kade Pieper and Trevor Lauck as early round draft picks. New QB Hank Brown will hand it off to RB Kamari Moulton, while WR Tony Diaz and TE DJ Vonnahme handle the receiving. Arkansas @ #20 Utah 7:15 pm on ESPN Eyes on: Arkansas has a new coaches and schemes. QB KJ Jefferson is big and fast with Chris Marshall as his go to receiver. title: Rams snap count review: Are the linebackers pulling their weight?
summary: After being out-coached, out-played, and yes, out-classed 27-7 by arch rivals, the San Francisco 49ers in their opening game, it is obvious that the Los Angles Rams have many holes to fill before they can begin to fulfill the high expectations that were bestowed upon them. TST pondered about three philosophies that could be holding […]
full_text: Quentin Lake #37 celebrates after intercepting a 49ers pass (Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) | Getty Images After being out-coached , out-played, and yes, out-classed 27-7 by arch rivals, the San Francisco 49ers in their opening game, it is obvious that the Los Angles Rams have many holes to fill before they can begin to fulfill the high expectations that were bestowed upon them. TST pondered about three philosophies that could be holding the Rams back. A fourth needs to be added. The thinking that undrafted linebackers are sufficient in today’s NFL. L.A.’s second line of defense was not only poor in Thursday’s loss, but has been a weak spot on a year-to-year basis. With the Rams moving away from the 5-2-4 defense of the early Sean McVay years to primarily four-man fronts, line backers have to be able step into holes and stack/shed blockers or at least clog up running lanes. It is particularly so for the L.A. unit, since they are not gifted in pass coverage. Names of players, their snap counts, and play percentage in bold. While the Rams trio of Nate Landman (64, 98%) , Omar Speights (30, 46%) , and Shaun Dolac (19, 29%) combined for 15 tackles, by my unofficial count, only one play, maybe two depending on how you grade things, was made within three yards of the line of scrimmage. Their tackles were coming four yards or more past the line, they need make stops for loss or no-gain. Defensive line Rough outing for the group as a whole, no one really stood out as having a strong game. The 49ers had a good pass plan, short and quick release, often one read. There was some pass rush pressure, but Purdy seldom had pressure up the middle into his face. S.F. ran the ball successfully both inside and off tackle. Kobie Turner (43, 66%) Poona Ford (33, 51%) Tyler Davis (32, 49%) Braden Fiske (29, 45%) Ty Hamilton (12, 18%) Edge How quiet was this unit? Aside from Myles Garrett, who was on the cusp of solid initial game, a total of seven tackles, five which were of the assist variety and none for loss, one QB hit, and zero sacks. Byron Young (47, 72%) Josaiah Stewart (28, 43%) Myles Garrett (40, 62%) Desjuan Johnson (15, 23%) Safety Quentin Lake (65, 100%) Solid game for Lake, he’s at his best on underneath coverage where his smarts and experience can be put to use. Covering the slot doesn’t allow a lot of wriggle room, whoever lines up there is who you cover, but I’d rather see Lake tracking the bigger receivers and tight ends. Over the long haul, he is likely to struggle vs the smaller shifty/fast receivers. Kamren Kinchens (52, 80%) Appeared to me that two of the S.F. passing touchdowns came when he lost track of coverage. It’s simply inexcusable when the deep center fielder in Cover3 lets a receiver run right by him for a big play. Jaylen McCollough ( 39, 60%) Another workman-like effort from the ex-Tennessee Volunteer. He plays a smart, steady brand of football. Strong guy to use in rotations/packages. Got in a lot of special teams work, too. Kamren Curl (30, 46%) Curl was off to a good start, but injured an ankle and did not return. Cornerback Trent McDuffie (65, 100%) Played about 25% of the time in man coverage and did very well. Liked the the way he stuck his nose in on run support as well as showing sticky coverage. Jaylen Watson (65, 100%) Drew Mike Evans and battled pretty well, albeit out-muscled on a pair of occasions. Still not a negative individual performance. Josh Wallace ( 7, 11%) Hardly noticed him in the game. What was more noticeable? Emmanuel Forbes did not get a sniff on defense. Special teams Returns and coverage. Does anything else need to be said? Quarterback Matthew Stafford (51, 84%) Rough game for Stafford, he seemed out of sync and his throws were off from the beginning. He seemed hell bent on throwing to his primary target, covered or not. How bad was it? Seven points was the lowest Rams scoring output in 75 games with Staff at the wheel. Staff did face a high 44% (11 of 25) pressure rate, but a handful of those came from him holding the ball too long. Stetson Bennett (10, 16%) Bennet did not look bad in the first real action of his career, but the 49ers had throttled things down by the time he entered the game. It was however, nice to see a Rams QB flash some athleticism and make some plays with his legs. Not sure why Stafford didn't throw this to Kyren in the flat. It was very good coverage by Lenoir, but this flat route has space, and I don't think anyone to the offense's right side is even expecting the ball pic.twitter.com/G5MNYQtF3c — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) September 11, 2026 Running back Kyren Williams (39, 64%) On a day when the Rams needed an offensive lift, the snap share clearly shows that the offensive braintrust regards Williams and his serviceable duty as RB#1. Blake Corum (14, 23%) Hmm. Corum gets in for 14 plays and carries the ball on on 10 of them, no telegraphing going on there. Still, he showed good vision and feel for holes, while having enough burst to make good gains. Ronnie Rivers (8, 13%) Don’t want to cry over spilt milk, but wasn’t a mop up situation like this tailor-made for a fast back with natural running skills and power, but little pro experience? A guy like Jarquez Hunter. You can’t argue that it’s about special teams, because Rivers didn’t take a snap in those areas. Wide receiver Puka Nacua (43, 70%) Would the Rams have had any passing offense without him? He made stellar grabs on two downfield passes, the Rams other completions were of the checkdowns and underneath variety. Davante Adams (33, 54%) He was open on occasions, but Stafford wasn’t close to hitting him. Jordan Whittington (25, 41%) Saw some good blocks out of Whit, but not really a an active part of the passing game. Did connect with Bennett later in the game for a catch over the middle. Didn’t add much in the kickoff return game. There wasn’t much Rams blocking, but he’s just not fast enough to work laterally. Konata Mumpfield (16, 26%) Quiet game for Mump, got his bell rung in the second half, but was able to return. I don’t see practice sessions, but it’s hard make a case for why Mumpfield is active over Atwell and/or Daniels. You could throw Brennan Presley in the that mix, too. Tight end Colby Parkinson (47, 77%) My biggest complaint about Parkinson is his lack of physicality. He seldom, if ever, lowers the boom on smaller tacklers and drives them. Not a great blocker either. When the offense stalls, like Thursday, these things tend to stand out. Terrance Ferguson (31, 51%) Just one target where he was covered and badly overthrown. Although most fans want to see him as a weapon, it’s good to see him working as a blocker as well. Davis Allen (21, 34%) Had one reception on a check down and turned it upfield for a nice gain. Suffered a possible concussion on the hit and left the game. Tyler Higbee (12, 20%) Played mostly after Allen was hurt. Caught a couple of short passes, but lost a fumble on a peanut punch. Offensive line A hit-and-miss performance. Their run blocking was quite good and the pass blocking was just okay. Some of the pass blocking woes were scheme-related, too many long-developing routes. Stafford held onto the ball way too long on few as well. McClendon had some struggles with Bosa but got after it in the run game. Alaric Jackson (61, 100%) Steve Avila (61, 100%) Coleman Shelton (61, 100%) Warren McClendon (61, 100%) Kevin Dotson (59, 97%) Beaux Limmer (2, 3%) 73 went toe’taggin last night 🏷️ pic.twitter.com/nEWp2e9rbR — Duke Manyweather (@BigDuke50) September 11, 2026 The good news As painful as it is to lose to the San Francisco 49ers, it is only one game and as pitiful as the pass game was, punching in that second half touchdown might have made a difference. No excuses though, the Rams came out flat and never got out of the funk. Who knows if the problem was the traveling protocols, a poor game plan, or just a pretty good ‘Niner team. The key now is to work on weak areas. The Rams look to have the…
