title: How will Miami Dolphins use Malik Willis in Week 1 against Las Vegas Raiders?
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are set to begin the 2026 season with a Week 1 matchup against the Miami Dolphins after both teams made significant offseason changes. To preview the game, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at The Phinsider, and Kevin Nogle was kind enough to answer a few questions about […]
full_text: (Photo by Lee Coleman/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are set to begin the 2026 season with a Week 1 matchup against the Miami Dolphins after both teams made significant offseason changes . To preview the game, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at The Phinsider, and Kevin Nogle was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Dolphins for Raider Nation. Q: From an outsider’s perspective, it looks like the Dolphins are entering a rebuilding season in 2026 (similar to the Raiders). What are the expectations in Miami for this year’s team? If making the playoffs is considered a long shot, what does a successful 2026 look like? A: I think, for the most part, if the Dolphins can look competitive, that will be seen as a win. We are all expecting a rough season, but there is hope that they can at least shock a few teams. Miami is set up to be everyone’s trap game this season, and they will be looking to take advantage of that. “I don’t think we have a choice, honestly,” linebacker Jordyn Brooks said last week when asked if the team was taking on an underdog mindset this season. “I don’t think there’s one outlet on social media, anybody that’s got us picked to win anything. Not that it matters, but that’s just what it is. I don’t think any of our opponents respect us, so 100% underdog mindset and I think that’s always the best position to be in. We’re going to carry that mindset into the season and have that ‘us against the world’ mentality and do our best to win football games.” This year really is a reset for the franchise. The front office is new. The coaching staff is new. The quarterback and much of the roster is new. Even the team president is new. They are also eating a record-setting $182 million in dead money this year to reset the salary cap. Miami is clearly in a reset, and the product on the field will likely look like it. Success for this year is if the team that takes the field in Week 18 looks and plays better than the team that hits the field on Sunday. This year’s primary objective has to be the growth and development of the roster’s 18 rookies, five first-year starters, and nine second-year players. Q: Malik Willis gets a chance to prove himself as a starting quarterback this season after spending the last two years backing up Jordan Love in Green Bay. How do you think new offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik will structure his scheme to fit Willis’ skill set? More specifically, the quarterback’s rushing ability? A: Slowik should run a Shanahan-style West Coast offense with elements of former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel’s scheme, but likely toned down, with less emphasis on speed, mismatches, and multiple pre-snap motion packages. There will still be motion, but it will be used to diagnose the defense rather than to create confusion or get wide receivers up to full speed before the snap. We probably will still see the rhythm-based passing game that was a McDaniel staple with quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, but Willis can take deeper shots and use power on his throws better than Tagovailoa could. I do think we will see Willis’ legs factor into the game plan. We only saw the Dolphins starters for one series in the preseason, and during joint practices the focus was on pocket passing and building chemistry, not moving Willis around or letting him take off on scrambles. I think we will see more read-option and designed quarterback runs enter into Miami’s offense. And Dolphins fans may learn they do not have to hold their breath any time the quarterback starts running. Q: De’Von Achane was a breakout performer in 2026 and earned a big payday in the offseason with a four-year, $64 million contract extension. How can he build on last year’s Pro Bowl campaign? If you were the Raiders’ defensive coordinator, how would you go about stopping (or just slowing down) Achane? A: Achane has said his goal is the NFL rushing title , and that might be reachable this season. To be fair, he said that is his goal every year, but 2026 might actually be the year he reaches it, given how much of Miami’s offense should run through him. The Dolphins have high expectations for the offensive line this season, which should only make Achane’s job a little easier. Opposing defenses know Miami’s offense centers on Achane, so they will stack the box to force Willis to throw. If they can get the passing game in any sort of rhythm, it should open lanes for Achane, which then makes the play-action that much more effective. It will all be cyclical, but it starts with Achane. Back to our discussion about Willis, the read-option will be a huge benefit for Achane. If defenses have to consider the possibility of Willis keeping the ball and running himself, it will cause them to hesitate, and that split-second could be all Achane needs to find space. And, finally, Slowik should get back to using Achane as a passing threat. There was discussion last year of Miami using him as their slot receiver; he could have that kind of impact in the passing game. It will not help him reach the rushing title goal, but I would expect a decent percentage of Achane’s touches to come through the air. To stop Achane, make sure you are disciplined in setting the edge. Slowik’s offense should look to stretch the field in the running game, taking advantage of Achane’s speed. Force him back into the middle, and keep your lane assignments covered. I think you were right with your assessment on Thursday: Quay Walker and Naokbe Dean will likely be the key . Stay clean, clog lanes, use Walker to offset some of Achane’s speed advantage, and be prepared for cutbacks. Q: Defensively, I was a little surprised to see that rookie Jacob Rodriguez will be wearing the green dot over 2025 first-team All-Pro Jordyn Brooks. What have you/the Dolphins’ coaching staff seen from Rodriguez during training camp and the preseason that led to that decision? How do the two linebackers complement each other on the field? A: I think I was more surprised that Brooks will not be calling the plays than I was that Rodriguez will be calling them. An All-Pro inside linebacker who was calling plays last year does not usually see that taken away from him, but I think it was twofold. First, Rodriguez earned it. Last week, Brooks said: “Jacob is, I like to say, like a rookie vet. He’s already seasoned. Whatever he was doing at Texas Tech, he was doing the right things. Came in very knowledgeable of the game, very mature and just ready to go. He’s just gotten better and better since OTAs, honestly. I’m excited to see his growth and what he does this year.” Brooks added to that on Thursday, saying: “No, he’s ready. I mean, he’s been ready. That’s why we trust him with the green dot. And so I think he’s come in ready and he’s just been getting better and better since he’s been here, since we drafted him. So I’m excited for his start and his contributions he will make for the defense and the team.” Defensive coordinator Sean Duggan explained the decision on Thursday, saying: “I think [Rodriguez]’s done a really nice job. It’s something he’s done since he’s gotten here. You know, he’s gotten better at it. I think the communication with him and [head coach Jeff Hafley] during the play call, getting kind of the rhythm of how he calls things has gotten better and better. Something I’ve appreciated about him is he’s been open about, ‘Hey, I kind of like it more said like this,’ and Haf’s like, well, ‘I like to say it like this.’ So it’s fun to see a rookie take that ownership of the call and that ownership of having the green dot on him. But he’s done a nice job, he really has. He’s gotten better and more comfortable with the playbook and with the calls and how to word it to the rest of the defense.” Second, I think you are probably going to see Brooks lining up as a weakside linebacker while Rodriguez will be in the middle. Giving Rodriguez the green dot and the…

title: Raiders Mailbag: Who needs to step up against Dolphins with Brock Bowers out?
summary: It’s been over eight months since we’ve seen a Las Vegas Raiders regular-season game, but that ends this weekend with the Week 1 matchup against the Miami Dolphins! This also kicks off (another) new era for the Raiders with Klint Kubiak’s first game as head coach and a revamped roster. However, Kubiak will be down […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been over eight months since we’ve seen a Las Vegas Raiders regular-season game, but that ends this weekend with the Week 1 matchup against the Miami Dolphins ! This also kicks off (another) new era for the Raiders with Klint Kubiak’s first game as head coach and a revamped roster. However, Kubiak will be down one of his best players with tight end Brock Bowers undergoing a “meniscus trim” on Tuesday, leading us into this week’s mailbag. Q: With Bowers out and Michael Mayer ascending to TE1, who will be TE2 and TE3? I assume Ian Thomas is TE2. Maybe Connor Heyward as TE3 or a practice squad call-up, bruv? Who else needs to step up? A: I think you’re correct that Thomas becomes the second tight end, and I’d imagine Heyward will be used similarly to how Kyle Shanahan deploys Kyle Juszczyk in San Francisco. According to Pro Football Focus , Juszczyk (I had to check the spelling three times and still got it wrong) actually spent more time as an in-line tight end than in the backfield last year (188 snaps to 167). Part of the reason for that was that George Kittle missed six games, so Juszczyk basically became the second tight end in the 49ers’ two tight end formations. In other words, Shanahan leaned on 21 personnel to run his 12 personnel packages since the fullback has such a diverse skill set. Obviously, Heyward isn’t the same caliber as the 10-time Pro Bowler, but they have similar traits to be used similarly. Heyward played both tight end and fullback at Michigan State, and he was used in-line a good amount during his first couple of seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers. So, he’s an option as the third and maybe even second tight end. Thomas is more of a blocker, so I could see Kubiak leaning on Heyward more in the passing game. That could eliminate the need to call someone up from the practice squad. But if that does happen, I’d imagine Chris Myarick gets elevated. Myarick hasn’t done much in his NFL career, but he’s been around for seven years to at least be a veteran option. Someone else asked if there is any chance Mayer steps up , noting his lack of agility and underwhelming blocking so far in his career. Before the Bowers news, I listed Mayer as one of eight players who are entering a “make-or-break” season this year . However, that’s not the case anymore after the shocking news about his three-year, $45 million contract extension. I’ll say this, though: After a big payday, it’s time for Mayer to hold up his end of the bargain and produce. And he now has a perfect opportunity to prove himself with the guy in front of him on the depth chart sidelined. To be clear, I’m not expecting Mayer to do everything that Bowers can do. There’s a reason we consider the latter a unicorn; he has a unique skill set that most tight ends don’t have. Also, they’re built fairly differently, with Mayer being taller, thicker and more physical, while Bowers is lighter, more agile, and has more finesse to be a separator as a receiver and make defenders miss after the catch. Will Mayer be split out wide and used from a variety of alignments in the offense, like how Bowers can be deployed? No, and it’d be unreasonable to expect that from him. However, this offense, especially the passing game, is supposed to go through Bowers. Meaning, with him out, there will be more opportunities for other pass-catchers to get targets, and Mayer has to take advantage of the balls that come his way. This Sunday will be the first test to see if Mayer can live up to the new contract. Along the similar lines, Tre Tucker needs to step up as well and prove that he can be a go-to receiver. He’s also in the final season of his rookie deal, and it’s going to take more than one player to replace what Bowers brings to the table. Q: With Bowers now out for a while, the schedule being what it is, this season could go off the rails quickly. Can you see Raiders throwing in the towel early and trading Crosby well before the deadline? A: Someone else asked if the trade deadline (Nov. 10) is the most important date on the Raiders’ calendar this year, and if guys like Maxx Crosby, Kolton Miller, Malcolm Koonce, Aidan O’Connell and Kirk Cousins will be on the trade block while players with lingering injuries (Jermod McCoy, Bowers, Ashton Jeanty) will get shut down. It’s weird to think of Week 1 as a swing game, but it kind of is for the Raiders this year. A little more on this in the next question; it’s hard to imagine Las Vegas winning many games if it can’t be a Miami team that completely revamped the organization in the offseason. Hypothetically, if the Raiders lose on Sunday, things aren’t getting any easier with road games against the Chargers and Saints in the next two weeks. If they’re heading into October at 0-3 with a matchup versus the Chiefs to begin the month, that could absolutely accelerate the process of the Silver and Black being sellers in the trade market. That being said, I think a Crosby trade would still depend more on whether another team is willing to meet John Spytek’s price tag. Maybe that isn’t two first-round picks anymore, but I’d imagine Spytek will want to be patient and field as many offers as possible to gain leverage. Then, timing becomes a factor, and it’d probably be the smarter wait as long as possible. Sure, he doesn’t want to lose a potential trade partner by them getting tired of waiting for Crosby and agreeing to trade for another edge defender from another team. However, contenders can get desperate as the trade deadline approaches and up their offer. Even if Spytek wants to move on from Crosby to pick up more draft capital, he can always wait until the offseason to make a trade. Crosby is under contract through 2029, and it’s arguably more beneficial to trade him after the draft order has been set so that the Raiders know exactly what they’re getting. When it comes to this year’s picks, at least. As far as the other guys listed above, I touched on Cousins and O’Connell last week. Check out the related article below for a more detailed answer. For the cliff notes: I think Cousins stays, but AOC will be on the block. When it comes to Miller, I’d keep him throughout the season. I like Charles Grant and could see a situation where Miller gets traded in the offseason to make room for Grant. But I’m not trusting a guy who has barely played in the NFL to protect Fernando Mendoza’s blind side during Mendoza’s rookie season. That’s the future of the franchise, and keeping him healthy is more important than picking up draft capital that you can’t use until the spring, anyway. Koonce’s situation might depend on Crosby’s. If the Raiders move on from the latter, then there’s room to re-sign the former, assuming he’s playing well enough to warrant a return. That being said, there is a world where both get dealt since Kwity Paye is on a three-year deal and the defense has a couple of young/long-term options at edge with rookies Keyron Crawford and Cian Slone. Crawford can’t play this season and Slone is on the practice squad, but I’m thinking of 2027 and beyond. As for resting players with injuries, I’d definitely consider shelving Bowers and honestly wouldn’t mind him getting put on IR (but designated to return) before Week 1. Meniscus injuries aren’t that devastating in the short-term, compared to an ACL or any of the other knee ligaments. However, a meniscus issue can get tricky when it comes to the long-term health of the knee. It can lead to issues with the other ligaments down the line, and Bowers already had the PCL injury in the same knee last year. I’m certainly not a doctor or even a medical expert, but I’d imagine the two injuries are at least somewhat related. So, in a season where expectations are already low and he’s already going to miss time, be smart and don’t rush him back on the field like the coaching staff did last year. The same logic goes for Jeanty, with the caveat being that a sprained ankle…

title: Raiders news: Tight end gets paid
summary: Michael Mayer will have one less thing to worry about as he begins the season as the Las Vegas Raiders starting tight end. His contract status is no longer a quesiton. Saturday morning, in a bit of a surprising move, the Raiders gave the prospective 2027 free agent a three-year contract extension worth a total […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Michael Mayer will have one less thing to worry about as he begins the season as the Las Vegas Raiders starting tight end. His contract status is no longer a quesiton. Saturday morning, in a bit of a surprising move, the Raiders gave the prospective 2027 free agent a three-year contract extension worth a total of $45 million with $30 million in guaranteed money according to NFL Media. The #Raiders have agreed to terms on an 3-year extension with TE Michael Mayer worth $45M with $30M guaranteed. The $15M APY ranks 4th among current TE contracts. The deal was negotiated by Kyle McCarthy, Brian Murphy, and Cam Hahn of @athletesfirst pic.twitter.com/Mlgqyp7kyl — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 12, 2026 It is a clear commitment to the tight end position by the Raiders. They fully see a future that will feature star Brock Bowers and Mayer for the foreseeable future in Klint Kubiak’s offense. Mayer, a second-round pick in 2023, is currently averaging the fourth highest contract for a tight end and he makes more money than any of the Raiders’ wide receivers. It is the highest three-year contract for a tight end ever. Bowers will very likely become the highest paid tight end in the NFL when he is eligible for an extension after this season. Bowers is currently out with a knee injury and Mayer will be the starter in the meantime. Mayer has had his moments, but consistency has been an issue. He has 83 career receptions with a high of 35 last season. The team clearly thinks he will elevate his game under Kubiak. Mayer is first Raiders’ draft pick to get an extension since Hunter Renfrow four years ago and is the first second-round pick since Derek Carr to be extended by the team. The Raiders’ 2027 free agent class wasn’t expected t feature many must-keep players. Now, with Mayer secured, perhaps the team will consider extending wide receiver Tre Tucker.

title: Fans confident in Dolphins direction as 2026 season begins
summary: The Miami Dolphins are expected to have a rough 2026 season as they reset their salary cap, roster, coaching staff, and front office in one year. Predictions for Miami range from 4 wins this year to not coming away with a single victory. It might be a tough year to be a Dolphins fan. The […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 21: Zach Sieler #92 of the Miami Dolphins runs on to field for the game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Hard Rock Stadium on December 21, 2025 in Miami Gardens, Florida. title: Miami Dolphins season 2026: Pattern recognition the key to success
summary: What do we look for on Sunday? Patterns. I am trying not to remember when the Baltimore Ravens scored numerous touchdowns against the Miami Dolphins during the first Brian Flores’ game against the Ravens. Remember what happened the next time we played the Ravens?  Coach Flores saw the pattern of their offense and devised a […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - AUGUST 28: Head coach Jeff Hafley of the Miami Dolphins looks on during the second half at Hard Rock Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images What do we look for on Sunday? Patterns. I am trying not to remember when the Baltimore Ravens scored numerous touchdowns against the Miami Dolphins during the first Brian Flores’ game against the Ravens. Remember what happened the next time we played the Ravens? Coach Flores saw the pattern of their offense and devised a weapon to stop it. Blitzkrieg city! We pushed the Ravens around that night. What patterns will we see on Sunday afternoon? And will we learn from them? Will there be Raiders running wild through the Fins secondary? Will Mr. Jeanty be hopping through numerous holes? Can our big Jonah re-energize himself and push the Raiders d-line around? This is start of the search for a new set of patterns. This leads me to three simultaneous processes that will occur during the game. Forgive me for the analogy that I must spring on you now. Please. These processes will be like the rivers at the Three Rivers Stadium where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers merge to form the Ohio river. Again, forgive me for even mentioning the Steelers (one day I will share my list of teams that I hate but now now). To complete the analogy: River one is coaching, River two is the player talent and the Ohio River is the Miami Dolphins as we see them right now. If one of the two source rivers recede then obviously the final product falls. We must have BOTH! This phenomenon is exactly what happened to Don Shula. I won’t go through the excruciating details of the fall of the greatest football franchise EVER. IMHO! If I dwell on it, I will get myself down. Hope and memories keep me going. The 17-0 season!!!! Andra Franklin and A.J. Duhe beating the hideous Jets and Richard Todd in the Southern Orange Bowl Swamp to go to the Super Bowl! In addition, I remember the pure excitement of Marino and the Marks Brothers. Sheer greatness! If you are too young to have seen it, I am sorry. To see the juggernaut Chicago Bears come into the Orange Bowl only to be destroyed on a Monday Night was the stuff of fairy tales. Many of you know the Monday night loss of the Bears was their only loss of the entire season as they would not lose again on their way to winning the Super Bowl. I will discuss that season ending pain (the suckiest January ever) at a different time as we progress. Enough looking back…for now. The question at hand is what on-field talent and coaching ultimately need to be improved. Some of you know intuitively that American football is the greatest game ever, not counting Yahtzee. Ha. Did you know Yahtzee was a game created by a woman on a…….yell it out….YACHT! When I learned that last year, I kicked myself…hard. What makes football the best sport ever is that we can grab the ball with our hands without a group of little guys pointing to their hands (Mommie, mommie he touched one square picometer of the ball…please give me a free goal) and there are 22 MEN on the field all at once and they make it look easy (usually) and those men crash into each other with full force (yes it’s brutal). I marvel at the team sport aspect: I truly think if you took last year’s SB Champ Seattle and had them play the best players hand-picked from each of the 31 other teams and gave that team only 2 weeks to prepare, Seattle would beat them handily. IMHO. I will explore this phenomenon more closely during the season. Back to the Fins, we cut loose Tyrel Dodson for the prospect of Jacob Rodriguez and cap room. Jacob will be a damned good player. Remember the last time we started a rookie Texas Tech linebacker, HOFer Zach Thomas? I was not sold on him because he was making “routine” inside linebacker plays during preseason. The NFL unemployment line is LITTERED with hundreds of LBs who could read runs and flow to the ball. That skill is common amongst that group of men. However, I was at Joe Robbie Stadium (I will always call it that) at Jimmy Johnson’s first game against the Patriots. The NE staff must have been thinking what I was thinking “He is a common linebacker making common plays, let’s run a reverse and expose him.” Shawn Jefferson was sacrificed to the football gods on the play and Zach Thomas sent him “Woozyheadville.” Zach was like a sidewinder missile with target lock when he knocked out Jefferson. I literally screamed in ecstasy just like I did when Bryan Cox (not the ORIGINAL Lecktor ) sent that jackass running back Harvey Thomas to “Woozyheadville” while he was with the Chiefs. So the Fins are putting “future permanent pieces” out for a trial by fire in real games. Jacob Rodriguez will make mistakes, all of our awesome rookies will. The “mistakes” that we can’t live with are not hustling, not learning the basics, not growing. We can live with mistakes from a future pro bowl linebacker who happens to play next to a current Pro Bowler, Jordyn Brooks. He will learn quickly and he will see the patterns of offense that we all have seen. If you recall, the year the Patriots went 17-0, they played the NY Giants and beat them 38-35, I do believe. After the Giants beat the Patriots like 4-5 weeks later in the Super Bowl, they said playing the Patriots in the regular season gave us a HUGE advantage for the Super Bowl. The Giants saw the patterns of what the Patriots did. Seeing the patterns and stopping the patterns are two different things but that Giants team had the right talent and coaching to beat one of the greatest teams of all time (yeah, right). The challenge for GM Sullivan and Coach Hafley is to put the best mix of players and coaches so that they can recognize patterns and defeat them. Go Fins!

full_text: Did you know the American lobster has a lifespan of about 15 years? That’s also the average lifespan of goats, cows, female lions and the small parrot known as the budgie. If you considered all of the lobsters, goats, cows, lionesses and budgies born in 2010, they will have lived their entire natural lives, all fifteen years, having witnessed only a single winning season from the New York Jets.* The Jets are an amazingly bad team. Admittedly, the Miami Dolphins aren’t looking that hot right now either, and we have our own streak of futility that we don’t need to get into here. But there’s a difference between a bad team and an unproven team, and right now, the Dolphins have so many question marks at every position (including the head coach) that they’re hard to quantify. They’re the NFL’s youngest team, so you have to assume growing pains, but are they Jets-level bad? Since we’re right on the cusp of the 2026 regular season, here are what various prognosticators are predicting for the Dolphins’ win total in 2026. I’ll offer my own take at the end, but throw your guesses in the comments. Former Dolphin Ryan Fitzpatrick : 0 wins! Sporting News : 2 wins Mike Clay, ESPN : 2.5 wins CBS Sports : 3.5 wins iHeart’s NFL Daily : 4 wins The Athletic: 4.4 wins Kalshi: 4.5 wins DraftKings: 4.5 wins BetMGM: 4.5 wins Hard Rock Bet: 4.5 wins ESPN : 4.5 wins Sports Illustrated : 4.5 wins Good Morning Football’s Peter Schrager: 5 wins Locked On Dolphins’ Kyle Crabbs: 5 wins 7 Oracles Predictions : 6.57 wins Gridiron Edge: 6.83 wins I know I tend to view the Dolphins with aqua-and-orange-tinted glasses, but I think the team’s offense has some real juice. The depth is a little scary, though, and I think like a quarter of the team just signed two weeks ago. Plus with so many first- and second-year players, it might look a bit ugly at times, especially early on. But you can put me down for 6 wins as the first step in a successful rebuild. How do you see the team finishing this year? Share your thoughts in the comments! *And to all those elderly lobsters and budgies born in 2011 hoping this is the Jets’ year: Don’t hold your breath.

title: Miami Dolphins draft prospects 2027: Who to watch for Oklahoma vs. Michigan
summary: Last week, I introduced a new post I am trying to add to The Phinsider this year, and it seemed to be well received. I would like to take a weekly look at one college football game on Saturday’s schedule and find players to watch who could be on the Miami Dolphins’ 2027 NFL Draft […]
full_text: NORMAN, OKLAHOMA - NOVEMBER 22: Defensive tackle David Stone #0 of the Oklahoma Sooners prepares to rush against the Missouri Tigers in the fourth quarter at Gaylord Family Oklahoma Memorial Stadium on November 22, 2025 in Norman, Oklahoma. Oklahoma won 17-6. (Photo by Brian Bahr/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, I introduced a new post I am trying to add to The Phinsider this year, and it seemed to be well received. I would like to take a weekly look at one college football game on Saturday’s schedule and find players to watch who could be on the Miami Dolphins’ 2027 NFL Draft radar. While the Dolphins have not started their 2026 season yet and we do not know when they will pick in the first round, I also do not want this to be only about first-round prospects. Because of that, you will find 10 players to watch in today’s Oklahoma at Michigan game, five for each. They range from a player who might be the first player at his position selected to players who may be waiting until day three to hear their names called. This game is heavy on defensive prospects, especially with players who could be day-one or day-two picks. Given that Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley came up as a defensive coach, this could be a scouting feast for Miami. Oklahoma 2027 Draft prospects David Stone, defensive tackle (Junior) – If he stays on track through this season, Stone will likely be the first defensive tackle off the board when the Draft kicks off. He feels like he was built in a defensive tackle mold, and he can play any role along the defensive interior. He plays with power, and he pushes into the backfield well. His primary focus has been on getting into the face and throwing lanes of opposing quarterback, so he needs to clean up run stuffing a little, but he can do that this year. He tends to rely on his bull rush more than anything else, so adding more to the repertoire will help his success at the NFL level. The Dolphins have spent several draft picks on defensive tackles in recent years, and if they select as early as predicted, Stone may not realistically be on their radar. Jayden Jackson, defensive tackle (Junior) – Stone is the top defensive tackle to watch, but Jackson could use that focus on the defensive line to make sure people see him as well. Jackson is probably better suited as a true nose tackle than playing a little further outside in the NFL, and he has to work on his pass-rush technique to make himself into a sure-fire prospect, but he can anchor against the run and clog up the middle of the defense. He should see one-on-one matchups this year as offenses scheme around Stone, so Jackson needs to flash to solidify his draft stock. Peyton Bowen, safety (Senior) – A likely day-two prospect, Bowen feels like a Swiss Army Knife kind of player who can work as a centerfielder, as a coverage player, or in run support. That could play perfectly into Hafley’s defensive scheme, but it might already have the better option in Kyle Louis. Bowen will gamble on making the big play and getting burned rather than making the sure play. Eli Bowen, cornerback (Junior) – The Dolphins’ secondary is the biggest question mark on the defense, and they could be looking hard at cornerbacks coming into the 2027 Draft. Bowen is likely a day-three pick, and he may be relegated to use only as a slot/nickel corner based on his size – a little smaller than Brent Grimes. He reacts and closes well and plays bigger than his actual size, but it probably is not enough to jump him up draft boards or turn him into a boundary or field option. He feels like someone who does everything you would want, but just cannot get past the size limitations, unlike Grimes. Taylor Wein, defensive end (Redshirt Junior) – Wein is not going to challenge for the top pass rusher in the Draft, likely coming in late on day two or early on day three. He has a fast first step, but he adds little technique after that. If he can avoid being stood up, he can make an impact, but he needs to add strength to fight through tackles and guards. Wein barely played his first two seasons at Oklahoma, then jumped into the starting lineup last year; another year of experience could be pivitol in his chances as a professional. He is probably a rotational player early in his NFL career, but the potential is there to add to his game with further development. Michigan 2027 Draft prospects John Henry Daley, defensive end (Senior) – Daley is an older prospect, having deferred college for service on a two-year mission before going to BYU. He then transferred a year later to Utah, where he spent two seasons, and then transferred to Michigan for this season. He relies on power as his pass-rush options, with little else behind that. He might sneak into the first round based on his past play, but a strong 2026 campaign could cement him there, especially if he adds more than just a bull rush to his arsenal. Andrew Sprague, tackle (Redshirt Junior) – Sprague has been stuck at right tackle throughout his time at Michigan, but he has the technique to switch to left if the Wolverines need it. He has the size and footwork needed to succeed in the NFL and on the left side, but his experience at right tackle could play into what the Dolphins need if injuries continue to be an issue with Austin Jackson. If Sprague continues to develop and adds some more strength this year, he could jump into the late first round, but he is likely a second-round pick right now if he declares for the Draft. Jyaire Hill, cornerback (Redshirt Senior) – Cornerback could be high on the Dolphins’ target list for 2027, and Hill could be in consideration. He is a fast corner who can play field or boundary, and he matches up well against receivers. His size and arm span allow him to get to the ball and break up receptions. He does not like to tackle, which will drag him down on draft boards, especially for a team that wants run support from cornerbacks. If he cleans up the tackling, he is a day-two prospect that could add size to a presumed area of need for the Dolphins. Zeke Berry, cornerback (Redshirt Senior) – Smaller than his teammate Hill, Berry makes up for it by just being nasty. He will go out there and just get it done. He can play in any role, but might be best suited as a slot/nickel corner in the NFL. He knows how to break up passes, especially with swatting the arms of a receiver right as the ball arrives – and his timing allows him to get away with it without a penalty. Like Hill, Berry has struggled with tackling. He does not provide much run support, and he has to clean up the finish once a catch is made. He is probably a day-three pick. Jake Guarnera, center (Redshirt Sophomore) – After a redshirt seasons in 2024, Guarnera started all season at right guard for Michigan last year, while he also filled in at center when needed; he was penalized only once and allowed just two sacks. He moves to center this year. Guarnera is an extremely solid prospect – he is not flashy and going to stand out, but he is not going to make mistakes either. That could be a perfect role for him in the NFL, where he might begin his career as a backup center/guard option, then develop into the reliable starter whose name you never hear – a good thing for an offensive lineman. He is probably a late day-three prospect.

title: Daily Norseman Roundtable: Know Your Enemy — The Detroit Lions
summary: The Minnesota Vikings start off the 2026 season with a rivalry game right away, and while that game is against the Green Bay Packers — more on that later — there’s no better time to get the lay of the land in the rest of the division than RIGHT NOW. Let’s talk about the Detroit […]
full_text: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - JULY 16: Jahmyr Gibbs attends Fanatics Fest NYC 2026 at Jacob Javits Center on July 16, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Bryan Bedder/Getty Images for Fanatics) | Getty Images for Fanatics The Minnesota Vikings start off the 2026 season with a rivalry game right away, and while that game is against the Green Bay Packers — more on that later — there’s no better time to get the lay of the land in the rest of the division than RIGHT NOW. Let’s talk about the Detroit Lions. They’ve run the gamut from good to great to mediocre in the last three years, and don’t have the distinct displeasure of playing the first-place schedule this year as they did last season. Will the real Detroit Lions please stand up? We asked the experts from Daily Norseman in our latest edition of the roundtable: The Lions have gone 12-5, 15-2 and 9-8 in the last three seasons — which/who of those are the REAL Lions? Brandon Warne : Of the three it’s probably 12-5, but again it’s a division where everyone will be biting kneecaps and as a result, I think most of the teams will gravitate toward that 9-8/10-7 ether. As an aside, it’s sort of wild how differently a 9-8 and 11-6 finish look when they’re literally one game of deviation from a 10-7 record. Anyway, I still think the Lions have more than enough talent on both sides of the football, but Terrion Arnold subtracted from the defensive side and David Montgomery on the offensive end should not be disregarded, either. This defense is the muckiest of muck piles and the Lions are right in the thick of it. Christopher Gates : I think the Lions have a decent amount of talent. I don’t think they’re 15-2 good, but I think they’re a bit better than the 9-8 that they showed last season, so yeah. . .I guess they’re closer to the 12-5 if we’re just going off of those three teams. I know they finished fourth in the division last year, but they still had a winning record and they’re probably in for a bit of a rebound this season, too. They’re definitely a team that shouldn’t be slept on. Warren Ludford : The 12-5 Lions are the closest version to this year’s Lions team. Their offensive line isn’t as good as the 14-3 version and the defense isn’t quite as good overall either. What Lions player do you feel is the most overrated? BW : Jameson Williams, though maybe it’s just because I see so many Lions fans convinced he’s in a completely different universe than Jordan Addison. The Lions, like the Bears, have immense talent on the offensive end but haven’t been able to get it all to sync up at the right time with health, suspensions and all of that — and Williams has been part of that. CG : This is a tough one because a lot of the Lions’ players who are highly rated actually are among the best in the league at their positions. If I had to pick one, I’d say someone like Sam LaPorta. He got off to a solid start in his first couple of seasons, but I don’t know if he’s in the “elite” tier of tight ends in the NFL or anything like that. Add to that the fact that he’s coming off a year where he dealt with back issues, and I think we may see him start to fall off a little bit. Of course, he’s still young enough that it might not affect him that much, but if I had to pick one of the bigger-name players on that roster, he’d be the one I’d lean towards. WL : Amon-Ra St. Brown. He’s a good slate route runner, but beyond that he doesn’t stand out as much, and yet he’s often mentioned as among the top tier despite his more limited route tree. How about underrated? BW : Jahmyr Gibbs. No matter how good you think he is, he’s better. CG : I know people like to talk down about him, but Jared Goff is better than a lot of people would like to admit, I think. He’s provided solid, steady play for the Lions since they brought him in to replace Matthew Stafford, and even though he’s been surrounded by pretty decent skill position talent, he’s been able to make decent use of it. Sure, he’ll still have the occasional moment where you’ll wonder what the heck he’s doing, but those aren’t nearly as frequent as people make them out to be. Goff doesn’t get enough credit for what he does in that offense, in my opinion. WL : Aiden Hutchinson. He’s been doing it without much help from the rest of the defensive line for a while now and still has great stats. What do the Lions do well that worries you most as a Vikings fan? BW : I don’t know if any team epitomizes the identity of their head coach more than the Lions, and that’s terrifying. As an observer, I kind of like the idea of a Madden-like coach throwing caution to the wind and going for it on 4th-and-3 in their own end just because they feel like it, and I like the idea that just because it’s conventional wisdom doesn’t mean it’s the only way to do things (or the wisest, as it were). But would I like to be a fan of that type of mindset? Man, I don’t know. I think I would, but maybe I’m built different. CG : The Lions are always aggressive, no matter the situation, which is something that’s generally pretty admirable. Yes, there have been times when Dan Campbell has made a call that’s come back to bite him squarely on the backside, but overall I would much rather have a coach get too aggressive than have a coach that’s too passive. At least when a coach is too aggressive, it’s because he believes enough in his team that he wants to give them an opportunity to go out and win the game themselves. It’s worked out for the Lions more often than not, and I’d like to see that sort of aggressiveness more frequently in Minnesota, to be honest. WL : When their offense is clicking, it’s hard to stop. What’s your record prediction for the Lions this season? BW : I’ll go with 11-6. They’ll split with the Vikings, and it’ll come down to the final week to see which team wins the NFC North crown. I want to believe it’ll be the Vikings, but if it isn’t them, I think it’ll be the Lions. CG : I think this division is going to end up coming down to the Bears and the Lions this season (and, yes, it still feels weird to say that). I said in the Bears roundtable piece that I think the Bears are going to end up taking the North for the second consecutive year, and I believe I put them somewhere in the 11-6/12-5 range, so I’ll put the Lions a game behind them in the 10-7/11-6 range. I’m not sure where the difference between the two of them will come from, but I just have the feeling that the Bears will somehow manage to pull it off. WL : 12-5. They have the easiest schedule in the league this season with two more easier games than other teams in the division that will help them a lot. But I feel like their window is closing.
author: Brandon Warne

title: Redemption With a Side of Reckoning
summary: It has been 250 days since the Minnesota Vikings beat the Green Bay Packers to end the 2025 season with a win over a bitter division rival. It was a tumultuous season that culminated in a shakeup of the entire front office. The 2026 offseason has been all about change and growth. For me personally, […]
full_text: It has been 250 days since the Minnesota Vikings beat the Green Bay Packers to end the 2025 season with a win over a bitter division rival. It was a tumultuous season that culminated in a shakeup of the entire front office. The 2026 offseason has been all about change and growth. For me personally, this offseason has been one of the more challenging professional journeys I have been on. Two days after the Vikings’ last game of the 2025 season, I received word that the company I worked for was closing my location. We were given three months to not only close a location down to the furniture and random tech junk, but to keep doing business as usual and continue serving our customers until the bitter end. If you work in the corporate world, you know that sometimes there are things out of your control. No matter how much effort you put in, no matter how many coaching conversations you have with your team, it is sometimes not enough. Much like the corporate world, the NFL is a cold, heartless place. I found myself over the summer sympathizing with Kyler Murray, who was in a similar, but quite different situation. We both seemed to be given the “it’s not you, it’s me” speech by our respective employers. We both hit free agency around the same time and had to find new homes. For me, that involved going through the interview process with multiple companies, one of which required 5 interviews (I didn’t get that job). It took months of searching and coming within days of moving even deeper into the belly of the enemy (southeast Wisconsin). Luckily, I found my fit locally and instead of having to uproot my family and leave behind everything we built for three years, I was able to land on my feet at a local institution that has great potential, that needed a shakeup to bring in the proper personnel. We don’t get infinite chances, and nothing is certain, so I am going full tilt to make sure I thrive in my role with my new company. For Kyler Murray, he was given an opportunity to resurrect his career with “quarterback whisperer” Kevin O’Connell. The Last Shot at Redemption It’s difficult to overcome when people doubt you or you are constantly facing rejection. No matter what happens, though, there is always opportunity for redemption. For me, that is the theme entering the 2026 NFL season. Careers, pride, and reputations are on the line this season. Starting at the top, Kevin O’Connell is in a “prove it” year where he needs to overcome the reputation of putting together great seasons, only to fizzle out in the first game of the playoffs. The first step taken was to put someone new behind center who, if he can even play marginally better than last year’s quarterbacks, can win games and lead the Vikings to the playoffs. Kyler Murray’s redemption arc could be an incredible one to watch. He started his career with the Cardinals winning rookie of the year and having nice seasons back-to-back. He has had the opportunity to throw to Hall of Famer Larry Fitzgerald and prime DeAndre Hopkins. However, since the departure of Hopkins, Kyler has not had the greatest supporting cast and played for a flailing organization that was grasping to keep even an ounce of relevancy in the NFL. In 2026, Murray will be throwing to, arguably, the best wide receiver in football, Justin Jefferson. It is hard to believe that 2026 will be a “redemption” season for Justin Jefferson, because he is a great player. However, 2025 definitely left a bad taste in his mouth and has people losing regard for him as the best receiver in football. People are forgetting how good he actually is, and I cannot wait to see him go absolutely NUCLEAR in 2026. Now I’m starting to get riled up! Overcome and Thrive The unit that most needs a redemption story is the offensive line. Last year’s debacle resulted in some of the worst protection and quarterback play from the Vikings in the last quarter-century. The front office’s spending spree didn’t make much of a difference. Signing Ryan Kelly turned out to be a complete disaster. In retrospect, it was a terrible signing of a player who didn’t have anything left in the tank. The revolving door at center, both in personnel and on game day, could not be more apparent. This season, the unit comes into the season reloaded and healthy. The smartest strategy the Vikings employed last season was easing Christian Darrisaw back into action and allowing him to hang up his cleats for the season once it was a lost cause. I look for him to come back at 100% and absolutely decimate any defensive lineman or linebacker who crosses his path. Will Fries is also two years removed from a major injury, and if he can return to form, alongside Brian O’Neill on the right side of the line, it is going to be fun to watch. The development of second-year guard Donavan Jackson will be one to closely monitor as well. Please, football gods, let Blake Brandel be the answer at center. Build an Identity On the other side of the ball, it isn’t so much a redemption arc incoming as it is a reckoning. A reckoning for NFL offenses that play against the purple and gold. We are about to witness the most Brian Flores defense that has ever Flores(ed) before. That sounded better in my head, but you get the idea. The defensive roster is now completely turned over from the abomination of Ed Donatell’s. This is Brian Flores’ defense. This is the Vikings’ defense. I don’t care if we win every game 6-3. I want to see this defense be the identity of the team and absolutely decimate its opponents. There are so many names of solid players on this defense, and we know it is going to be schemed up in ways that frustrates opposing offenses and renders them ineffective. From my perspective, I see an intelligent, veteran defense with an injection of youth. We have seen over the past few seasons that rookies are eased into Flores’ system, and I think that trend will continue this year. I can’t wait to see Big Citrus and Caleb Banks in midseason form. Dallas Turner is going to be beastly. My favorite Viking of all time, Harry the Hitman, is back for one final season (never a doubt he was coming back). He is the heart, soul, and brain of the entire defense. I’m so glad he gets one more shot at a deep playoff run. I want every Sunday to be a nightmarish hellscape for opposing offenses, and I think my wish will be granted. It’s Time! The struggle bus is making its last stop. It’s time for you, me, and the Minnesota Vikings to embark on a new journey in a freight train of grit and determination. Wear your purple and gold proudly. If anyone asks you what you think of this year’s Vikings, just smirk and say, we’ll see. Not, like, in a cocky way, but more with calm, cool confidence. We have all worked hard to get where we are in life. Have the confidence in yourself that you can persevere and achieve your goals. Envision the life you want, envision the season you want to witness, and never stop believing in this team. After months of radio silence, I am ready to return as the overenthusiastic and positive Vikings fan. I am so excited to drink the tears of entitled Green Bay Packers fans! The Gjallahorn will be music to my ears and my sign that everything is right in the universe. It’s FOOTBALL SEASON!!!!!! Let’s GOOOOOOOOOOOO! SKOL
author: Jesse M

title: Why the Vikings Hold Their Best Advantage Over the Packers in Five Years
summary: The Minnesota Vikings kick off 2026 with their fourth different starting quarterback in four years — Kyler Murray takes the reins as Kevin O’Connell attempts to elevate yet another veteran signal-caller. On this episode of Two Old Bloggers, Dave Stefano and Drew Bunting (filling in for Darren Campbell) dive deep into what it takes to […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - JANUARY 04: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings signals a first down during the first quarter against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings kick off 2026 with their fourth different starting quarterback in four years — Kyler Murray takes the reins as Kevin O’Connell attempts to elevate yet another veteran signal-caller. On this episode of Two Old Bloggers, Dave Stefano and Drew Bunting (filling in for Darren Campbell) dive deep into what it takes to be a Super Bowl contender, using Matthew Coller’s 10-year analysis: 80% of Super Bowl teams scored 450+ points, 90% had a QB rating above 95, and 85% rushed for over 1,700 yards. Dave noted, “Kevin O’Connell has never hit 450 in a season,” while Drew demanded more offensive aggression: “Why aren’t the Vikings flirting with 30 points a game every week? You have 10 to 12 possessions, you have these great players. What the hell are we doing?” Flores’ defense already meets contender benchmarks — every Flores season has held opponents under 362 points. The offense? Still chasing. The Packers arrive wounded — without Josh Jacobs (commissioner’s list) and Micah Parsons (PUP), plus an offensive line in flux. Green Bay replaced 20 coaches and lost roughly 11 key roster pieces. Drew was blunt: “No Jacobs and no Parsons. The Vikings are at home facing a team who doesn’t have their best offensive player and doesn’t have their best defensive player. You can’t lose this game.” He ranked Green Bay’s offensive line 27th versus Minnesota’s 12th, giving the Vikings an 8-to-10-point edge. The turnover battle looms largest — KOC’s Vikings are 33-5 when winning or tying the turnover margin, and 5-20 when losing it. As Drew put it: “When you got a double-digit lead, somebody needs to tell KOC that’s when you go for the throat.” Prediction: Vikings by four or five, or 8-to-10 points. Key Points: QB Carousel: Murray is the 4th opening-day starter in 4 years. Dave: “That’s not a plan, it’s a personality trait.” Super Bowl Benchmarks: 450+ points, 95+ QB rating, 1,700+ rush yards. KOC has topped out at 432. J.J. McCarthy Demoted: Carson Wentz named backup; McCarthy runs scout team. Darren believes this may be J.J.’s last season in purple. Harrison Smith Returns: The Hitman, Year 15, is one INT shy of tying Ed Sharockman’s franchise record of 40. Drew: “He’s a coach on the field. That’s worth the signing right there.” Jihad Ward Re-signed: Flores collects veteran edge rushers like Pokémon cards. Drew: “You don’t get to the playoffs without depth.” Packers Decimated: 20 coaching changes, ~11 roster departures, no Jacobs, no Parsons, O-line ranked 27th. Win the Turnover Battle or Die: Vikings are 33-5 when winning the turnover battle, 5-20 when losing it. NFC North Beast: Drew predicts all four teams reach double-digit wins. Prediction: Vikings by 8-10; the under is the recommended bet. Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: This is the best matchup advantage Minnesota has had against Green Bay in five years, but as Drew warns, “It’s the Vikings, so in the fourth quarter when it’s 13 to 13, we’re all texting each other.” Can KOC finally let loose and score 30? Can Murray silence the doubters in his debut? Tune in to Two Old Bloggers every week on Vikings 1st & SKOL, part of the Bleav Network — because football’s back, and so are your two old bloggers. SKOL! Fan With Us! We have your Minnesota Vikings talk amongst the Two Old Bloggers , Darren @KickassblogVike and Dave @Luft_Krigare . Join the conversation! Fan with us at Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and the at the @BleavNetwork . What’s Your Prediction: Vikings domination or another nail-biter?
author: David Stefano

title: Vikings Elevate Kyle Van Noy, DeeJay Dallas for Sunday’s Game
summary: Even though there are no members of the Minnesota Vikings with an injury designation going into Sunday’s season opener against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium, the team has elevated two veterans from the practice squad to the active roster for Sunday’s game. The team has announced that it has elevated both running […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - JANUARY 04: Baltimore Ravens linebacker Kyle van Noy (53) looks on during the NFL football game between the Baltimore Ravens and Pittsburgh Steelers on January 4, 2026 at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh, PA. (Photo by Mark Alberti/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Even though there are no members of the Minnesota Vikings with an injury designation going into Sunday’s season opener against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium, the team has elevated two veterans from the practice squad to the active roster for Sunday’s game. The team has announced that it has elevated both running back DeeJay Dallas and outside linebacker Kyle Van Noy to the active roster for the season opener. Dallas will provide some depth in the backfield for the Vikings behind Jordan Mason, Aaron Jones, and Demond Claiborne. He also has some skills in the return game and could be used in that capacity next to Myles Price as well if the team chooses to do so. He hasn’t gotten a lot of carries out of the backfield in recent seasons, so perhaps the return game is where we’ll see him used the most. Van Noy, who will likely be a permanent fixture on the active roster sooner rather than later, will likely serve as one of the primary backups to Dallas Turner and Andrew Van Ginkel. He has experience with Brian Flores’ defense, having played for Flores in both New England and Miami, and has spent the past week and a half or so getting reacquainted with the defense after signing with the team after final cuts were made. This is, obviously, the first elevation for both of these players this season. Players are allowed to be elevated from the practice squad to the active roster three times during the regular season. After that, they must be signed to the active roster if teams want to continue using them on game days.

title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Confidence Not Sky High to Start 2026 Season
summary: The results are in for the first SB Nation Reacts polls of the regular season for our Minnesota Vikings, so let’s take a look at how everyone is feeling on the eve of the new campaign. We had two questions for you this week, with the first one being the question that we’ll be asking […]

(Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The results are in for the first SB Nation Reacts polls of the regular season for our Minnesota Vikings, so let’s take a look at how everyone is feeling on the eve of the new campaign. While the number is above the 50% mark, it isn’t quite as high as we’ve seen it at the start of seasons in the recent past. Of those who responded to our poll, 60% feel that the team is, in fact, moving in the right direction. As we’ve generally stated, this can mean different things to different people, but there are still a lot of questions that need to be answered about our favorite squad as we head into the season opener. Hopefully we’ll get some positive answers to those questions on Sunday afternoon against the hated Green Bay Packers. Speaking of that matchup, our other question for this week was how you think the purple will fare in their first game of the season. Our readers feel, overwhelmingly, that our team will come out with a victory, though the margin seems to be up for some debate. Of those who responded to our poll for this week, 48% believe that the Vikings will emerge victorious by a touchdown or less, while another 34% believe that they’ll win by an even greater margin. So, 82% of those who responded to our question for this week believe that our favorite team will be getting off to a 1-0 start to the 2026 season, which is nice. Of those who believe that the Vikings will be starting 0-1, the numbers. . .which somehow add up to 101% rather than 100% because of rounding errors (I assume) that I haven’t seen. . .have a slight lean towards the Vikings losing by more than a touchdown than they do toward them losing by less than that. If you saw my post on the prop bets for this one that I put up late last night, you’ve seen my prediction. I’ve already said that the Vikings will win, but I don’t think it’s going to be in blowout fashion or anything, so put me in the majority on this one. I think the purple take this one home by less than a touchdown. Let’s call it 24-20 or something along those lines. Those are our SB Nation Reacts results for this week, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you, as always, to everyone who took the time to participate in our poll for this week, and keep your eyes open for next week’s questions! title: Daily Norseman Roundtable: Know Your Enemy — The Chicago Bears
summary: The Minnesota Vikings start off the 2026 season with a rivalry game right away, and while that game is against the Green Bay Packers — more on that later — there’s no better time to get the lay of the land in the rest of the division than RIGHT NOW. Let’s talk about the Chicago […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears against the Cincinnati Bengals during the preseason game at Paycor Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings start off the 2026 season with a rivalry game right away, and while that game is against the Green Bay Packers — more on that later — there’s no better time to get the lay of the land in the rest of the division than RIGHT NOW. Let’s talk about the Chicago Bears. One year after finishing 5-12, the Bears almost completely flipped the script in their maiden voyage under Ben Johnson, going 11-6 and winning the NFC North before falling at Soldier Field to the Los Angeles Rams in the Divisional Round. Were the Bears for real last year? Is a straight shot back to the top of the NFC North imminent for the Windy City Warriors? We asked the experts from Daily Norseman in our latest edition of the roundtable: I’m feeling distinct 2023 Vikings vibes from this Bears team, thoughts? Brandon Warne : I guess it’s kind of weird for me to reply to this considering I also asked the question, but hear me out a bit: I don’t think any team will ever go 13-4 again with a negative point differential. But at the same time, the Bears were 11-6 with just a plus-26 point differential. By expected wins and losses, that should look more like a 9-8 team — and now one that has to play not only a difficult NFC North slate, but a first-place schedule, besides. Here’s a list of teams who have won 11 or more games with a point differential worse than the Bears’ plus-26 last season: 2012 Colts (11-5, minus-30) 2020 Browns (11-5, minus-11) 2022 Vikings (13-4, minus-3) 2004 Falcons (11-5, plus-3) 2023 Eagles (11-6, plus-5) 2019 Seahawks (11-5, plus-7) 2014 Cardinals (11-5, plus-11) 2003 Panthers (11-5, plus-21) That’s not many. Four of those teams finished .500 or worse the next season — the 2004 Panthers, 2005 Falcons, 2021 Browns and of course, the 2023 Vikings. Then again, the Eagles won 14 games, the Cardinals won 13, the Seahawks 12 and the Colts 11. There’s definitely a divide — I just think I have the Bears more in the first group than the second, with added emphasis on a tough divisional schedule along with a first-place schedule, besides. The Lions played that schedule last season and ended up 9-8, which feels about right for this Bears group. Christopher Gates : I think the Bears are a bit different from the 2022 Vikings in that the Bears only had one game last season where they really got thumped, and that came against the Lions in Week 2, after that incredibly deflating loss to the Vikings in Week 1 on Monday night. When the 2022 Vikings lost, they went out and got the crap beaten out of them and managed to finish the season with a negative point differential despite going 13-4. Now, if Caleb Williams goes down for the Bears the way that Kirk Cousins went down for the Vikings in 2023, all bets are off, because I don’t think the Tyson Bagent Experience™ would be able to push them to nearly the heights that Williams is capable of. Absent that, however, I think this Bears team is a lot better positioned than that Vikings team was. Warren Ludford : Yeah, I suspect the Bears will fall back considerably this year. I’m guessing 7-10 record. They have a much more difficult schedule than last season and led the league in takeaways and had the fewest giveaways. Reversion to the mean could be significant. Shawn C : Maybe, though I’d argue that injuries derailed the Vikings more than anything in 2023. If Cousins hadn’t gone down on that crappy Lambeau Field turf, I think they’d have returned to the playoffs. It just seems like the Bears have a unique ability to pull off random, magical seasons, then quickly revert to form. Think 2001, 2006, 2010, 2018, etc. I do think the Caleb Williams-Ben Johnson combo is legit, so maybe this will prove more lasting. I just don’t see their absolutely ridiculous +22 turnover differential (five more than the 2nd-place Texans) being repeated. What Bears player do you feel is the most overrated? BW : It’s Caleb Williams for me. The Jordan Love-esque 27-7 TD-to-INT ratio belies a scattershot accuracy that I just can’t see being sustainable over another full season. Sure, he can grow and improve — look at Love and Josh Allen as examples — but I don’t think it’ll be without some growing pains at first. I’m expecting a bumpy year from Williams. CG : Rome Odunze. I know the rule used to be that it took wide receivers coming out of college a couple of years to adjust to the NFL, but that has gone increasingly by the wayside in recent years, and while Odunze has been productive in spurts, he hasn’t really wowed anyone through his first two seasons. Maybe “overrated” isn’t the right word for Odunze, but even though the Bears’ passing offense hasn’t been as high-flying as a lot of teams in his first two years in the NFL, for a guy who was taken with a top-ten selection, I guess you’d just expect more than ~1400 yards in two years. Perhaps now that D.J. Moore has been dealt to Buffalo, those numbers will go up a bit, but people now seem to be in love with Luther Burden, so he may cut into any potential targets Odunze might get instead. WL : Caleb Williams. He was one of the least accurate starting quarterbacks in the league last year, yet some consider him a top-10 QB. SC : Dayo Odeyingbo, given the contract. Before the season-ending injury, he hadn’t performed up to his potential. It’s a big year for him. With the secondary losses, Odeyingbo and the defensive line will play a major role in the Bears’ success or failure this season. How about underrated? BW : I don’t know if it counts, but I wrote the questions so I’m going with it anyway — it’s Ben Johnson and the situation he’s set up for Williams and the offense. It feels like the perfect offensive yin to Brian Flores’ defensive yang as it pertains to building a system with personnel fits tailored to players and vice versa. Put Williams in a bubble and you can massage some of his inadequacies and inaccuracies in a way that still allows a team to win. Of course, I also think a lot of this applies to Kevin O’Connell, and while I’m still a huge fan, there have definitely been periods of transition in his tenure as well. CG : He doesn’t get as much ink as a lot of running backs do, but D’Andre Swift has been a pretty solid back in this league for a long time. He’s been a 1,000-yard guy in two of the last three seasons and led the Bears in touchdowns last year. I know a lot of people are high on Kyle Monangai, and for good reason, but Swift is the sort of steady presence an offense needs. He’s also usually good for about 50-60 catches a year, which is something that can’t be discounted. As I said, if you make a list of the top running backs in the NFL, Swift probably isn’t one of the first names you’re going to mention, but he’s definitely somewhere in the top half, in my opinion. WL : Colston Loveland is pretty good, probably not talked about enough. SC : Jonah Jackson. Everything Ben Johnson wants to do depends on dominant offensive line play. Jackson was very good last year and was instrumental in the Bears’ offensive improvements. Vikings fans are well-versed in the highs and lows of the Garrett Bradbury experience, and Jackson will be needed to anchor the interior. What do the Bears do well that worries you most as a Vikings fan? BW : They mask their issues well. They have two solid backs and a quarterback you have to account for. What their pass-catching corps lacks in experience and, at times, durability, they make up for in electricity. The defense is hard-nosed and had a few of the splash plays like the 2022 Vikings did which spurred them to that incredible, if a bit unusual, season. CG : They run the football. A lot. And they’re really good at it. When people think of Ben Johnson, they usually think of the sort of high-flying offense that he ran when he…

title: Defensive head-to-head preview: Saints vs Lions
summary: The Saints kick off the 2026 season on the road against the Detroit Lions. This matchup will be an early test for a young Saints team that is looking to establish itself as a contender for the NFC South division. The Saints finished off 2025 with one of the best defensive units in the league […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TN - DECEMBER 28: New Orleans Saints defensive end Chase Young (99) sacks and steals the ball from Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) during a game between the Tennessee Titans and New Orleans Saints, December 28, 2025, at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Matthew Maxey/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Saints kick off the 2026 season on the road against the Detroit Lions. This matchup will be an early test for a young Saints team that is looking to establish itself as a contender for the NFC South division. The Saints finished off 2025 with one of the best defensive units in the league and were able to showcase some flashes of that throughout the preseason, even after having some key losses in the offseason. Statistically, the Saints hold an advantage over the Lions. The Lions finished 2025 as the 18th-ranked overall defense under first-year DC Kelvin Sheppard. The Lions gave up 24.3 points per game, 217 passing yards per game, and 114.5 rushing yards per game. Now, the Lions were able to get four more sacks on the season than the Saints had. The Lions will feature an attacking 4-3 defense, shifting into a 4-2-5 style to match up when offenses switch to more pass-friendly sets. While, on the whole, the Lions defense is middle of the road, their pass rush is really good. Not only did the Lions have 49 sacks, but they were also able to complement the pass rush by forcing 13 interceptions. The advantage for the Saints is that the Lions will be missing three former starters in their secondary. Corner Terrion Arnold was released from the team due to his off-the-field issues, and both safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are on the PUP list. Kellen Moore and Tyler Shough must be able to take advantage of this secondary on Sunday if they are going to win this game. The Saints, on the other hand, are entering this game missing some pieces, but overall, they are pretty healthy on the defensive side of the ball. Brandon Staley is entering his second season as the Saints DC, and Saints fans, this could very well be his final year if things go as well as they did last season. Staley was really good, and with another year in this system, it is only fair to expect his defense to take another step forward. The Saints finished ninth overall in total defense in the NFL. The Saints will need to ensure that the rushing defense improves, and the addition of rookie DT Christen Miller will help with that, as well as provide some much-needed interior pass rush. The Saints will have to disrupt the timing of Jared Goff. Goff got rid of the ball with one of the league’s fastest releases at 2.57 seconds. Goff does not like to move, and if he can be forced off his platform and his timing disrupted, the Saints can impose their will on the Lions offense. The defensive matchup will be very fun to watch. It feels good to break down a game that will result in an actual win or loss for the season. Football is officially back. Share with us who you think has the advantage on the defensive side of the ball. Do you think Shough and Moore can expose the secondary? Are you concerned that Kelvin Sheppard’s unit will show some improvement against the Saints to start the season? Share your thoughts in the comments.
author: Anthony Parker

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Lions
summary: Look how far we’ve come! It’s officially NFL season, and the New Orleans Saints will travel to Michigan to take on the Detroit Lions at Ford Field. The Lions are currently 6.5-point favorites. Despite leading the way in predictions to come out with the win, Sunday’s matchup is very winnable for the Black and Gold. […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - DECEMBER 14: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter at Caesars Superdome on December 14, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Look how far we’ve come! It’s officially NFL season, and the New Orleans Saints will travel to Michigan to take on the Detroit Lions at Ford Field. The Lions are currently 6.5-point favorites. Despite leading the way in predictions to come out with the win, Sunday’s matchup is very winnable for the Black and Gold. By utilizing their strengths and taking advantage of these key matchups, the Saints could start the season 1-0. Saints WRs vs. Lions’ Secondary There is one glaring way the Saints can win on Sunday, and it all revolves around the Lions’ secondary. Detroit will be without their starting safety pair, Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, along with losing their former first-round pick, Terrion Arnold, after off-field issues. On the flip side, New Orleans totally revamped their receiver room in the offseason, adding three wideouts in the draft. While the star of the offseason, Jordyn Tyson, won’t be active for the game as he deals with an injury, Bryce Lance and Barion Brown have each made their own waves during training camp, opening a big opportunity for them to stand out in their NFL debuts. And of course, we can’t talk about the Saints receiver room without bringing up their $124 million man in Chris Olave. The fifth-year wideout is poised for his biggest season yet with his growing connection with Tyler Shough. Olave was Shough’s go-to target during the team’s 4-1 stretch to end the season, and that connection has only grown through the offseason and training camp. With promising rookies, the star power of Olave, and the return of Devaughn Vele, New Orleans’ wideouts should have a big day in the season debut. Saints run defense vs. RB Jahmyr Gibbs The inevitable decider of the game will be determined by the Saints’ ability to slow down running back Jahmyr Gibbs. The consensus first-overall pick in fantasy football is poised to have a big season with Detroit moving on from veteran running back David Montgomery, handing the keys of the offense to their fourth-year superstar. The Saints were solid against the run in 2025, but will be missing a key piece to that run defense. Demario Davis left in free agency to rejoin the New York Jets, leaving a large hole in their defense. New Orleans, however, swiftly replaced Davis with Kaden Ellis. While Ellis isn’t the same caliber of player as Davis, he is one of the top players at his position in the league and slots in nicely for the Saints. The Lions offense is full of firepower. Outside of Gibbs, Jared Goff has Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, and Sam LaPorta as weapons. Despite this, the Black and Gold significantly increase their chances of winning by slowing down the run game and forcing the Lions through the air, but it definitely won’t be easy. Saints run game vs. Lions run defense Detroit will certainly try to expose the Saints’ offense in Week 1, likely by taking advantage of the inexperience at quarterback. While team’s respect Shough a lot more after his hot finish to the season, the age-old tendency says to blitz the young quarterback. For the Saints to counter this, they’ll need to establish the run, something they emphasized in the offseason. New Orleans brought in star running back Travis Etienne and signed David Edwards to a big contract. These moves were made shortly after free agency opened, emphasizing that the Saints want to build on their run game. While the Lions have made some improvements to their run defense, they ranked in the bottom half of the league in 2025, allowing 4.4 yards per carry. If the Saints can get a strong run game established with Etienne, it will open up the offense for their young quarterback and take the pressure off.
