title: College Players to Watch: Week 1
summary: With the 2026 season set to kick off tomorrow, the Saints are looking to make a run at winning the division, but that does not mean they will not also be preparing for the upcoming 2027 NFL Draft and evaluating what improvements they will need to make to increase the overall quality of the roster. […]
full_text: AUSTIN, TX - APRIL 18: Edge Colin Simmons #1 of the Texas Longhorns warms up during the Texas Longhorns Football Fan Day on April 18, 2026, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With the 2026 season set to kick off tomorrow, the Saints are looking to make a run at winning the division, but that does not mean they will not also be preparing for the upcoming 2027 NFL Draft and evaluating what improvements they will need to make to increase the overall quality of the roster. Here are a few players to keep your eye on today as college football games get underway. Many draft analysts are expecting the Saints to be in the market for an elite edge rusher, and the name that has been closely associated with the Saints this summer has been Colin Simmons. Simmons plays for Texas and is a well-known prospect, especially among LSU fans, as LSU was almost able to get him to commit over the University of Texas. Simmons will be facing off against top-ranked Ohio State today in a primetime matchup. Simmons is currently ranked as the No. 1 edge rusher in the upcoming draft. Another name to watch at the same position is South Carolina edge rusher Dylan Stewart. Many experts see Stewart as the primary player who could challenge Simmons for that No. 1 edge spot in the draft. Stewart is viewed as a high-upside prospect. As a true freshman, he finished with 6.5 sacks, but even more impressive was his 91.4 pass-rush grade from PFF. Stewart will be facing off against Towson at 6 p.m. Staying with the edge rushers, keep an eye on Jordan Ross. The SEC Defensive Player of the Week in Week 1 may not currently be considered a first-round pick, but he is a player who could find his way to the Saints if they decide to go with a different position earlier in the draft. Ross is in his third season and was an elite five-star prospect who spent his first two years at Tennessee. In his first game with the Tigers, Ross finished with one sack, a pick-six, two tackles for loss, four total tackles and a quarterback hurry. Here is a position group the Saints could, and may actually, explore in 2027: tight end. LSU has the No. 1-rated tight end in the country in Trey’Dez Green. First, the narrative of keeping a Louisiana native home and potentially drafting him early would be a great story. Second, he would fill an immediate position of need depending on what happens with current tight end Juwan Johnson, who would be entering the final year of his contract next season. Green also adds versatility to the offense. He can provide some in-line blocking, but you can also flex him out, where he would provide a more explosive receiving threat than what the Saints currently have in the tight end room. Ross and Green will both be at home tonight as LSU faces Louisiana Tech at 6:30 p.m. Finally, there is Notre Dame cornerback Leonard Moore. Moore enters the 2026 season as the No. 1-rated cornerback in the upcoming draft class. He could give the Saints the immediate lockdown corner many feel the team does not currently possess. Moore finished the 2025 season with five interceptions and seven pass breakups while earning a 91.8 overall defensive grade and a 92.5 coverage grade from PFF. He is, quite simply, a shutdown corner. Moore and Notre Dame will line up against Rice today at 2:30 p.m. Who are some other players you would like to keep an eye on this weekend? Share your thoughts with us below in the comments.

title: Jaxson Dart holds NY Giants’ future in his hands, wants to do ‘something special’
summary: John Harbaugh is the biggest reason for the optimism around the New York Giants entering the 2026 season. Jaxson Dart, though, holds the key to just how bright the Giants’ future might be. This is something I said this week during an appearance on the ‘NFC East Mixtape’ podcast: “Everything starts for the Giants with […]
full_text: John Harbaugh and Jaxson Dart | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co John Harbaugh is the biggest reason for the optimism around the New York Giants entering the 2026 season. Jaxson Dart, though, holds the key to just how bright the Giants’ future might be. This is something I said this week during an appearance on the ‘ NFC East Mixtape ’ podcast: “Everything starts for the Giants with John Harbaugh. You guys know what the Giants have been for the last 12, 13 years. It hasn’t been pretty. It has mostly not been enjoyable. There are warts on John Harbaugh’s resume from Baltimore. We know that. But John Harbaugh brought credibility. He brought culture. He brought leadership. He brought professionalism and an idea for how to build a football team that this organization badly needed. So everything changes with John Harbaugh. Everything starts with John Harbaugh. “It doesn’t go where the Giants want it to go unless Jaxson Dart is what they think he can be at some point in the future. So, it starts with with Harbaugh, but if they’re going to get where they want to be, it runs through Jaxson Dart.“ Dart’s potential is one of the reasons Harbaugh took the Giants job. In a fascinating sitdown with former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin, Harbaugh said Dart is “even more talented than I thought he was.” “When you watch a player every day in practice, you get a sense of what he’s capable of doing. He can really throw it,” Harbaugh told Tomlin. “He really has a great pocket presence. He understands the pocket. He feels it. He also sees downfield. Then he can get out and move and he can make plays. He’s got a patience and poise about him.” That doesn’t mean Dart, a second-year quarterback with 12 NFL starts on his resume, is where the Giants need him to be. “He’s learning,” Harbaugh said. “Our coaches are doing a great job with him every single day. He’s got to find a way to be tight and refined like all the quarterbacks do. But you don’t want to take away. You never took it away from Ben [Roethlisberger] … “… There’s times that they’ll just they’ll look at you and you’ll know. It’s like, “Hey, man, I trust you.” You go be you.” ‘Backyard football’ isn’t enough In his annual quarterback rankings , Chris Simms of NBC Sports had Dart at No. 22. That is one spot ahead of Cam Ward of the Tennessee Titans, and one spot behind Jalen Hurts of the Philadelphia Eagles. In an exclusive interview with Big Blue View, Simms said his biggest long-term question about Dart is whether he will ever be an elite thrower of the football. “Dart’s got unreal feel and instincts, right. And his ability to extend plays and play backyard football is really where he’s special, and really a part of his game that I did not see that coming from what I evaluated in college,” Simms said. “He’s a pretty good decision-maker. “I like his arm. I’m just saying I don’t know if it’s elite. I’m not sure it’s an elite arm. It’s a real good arm.” Simms said Dart “hits the throws that are there to be made.” Simms just isn’t certain the 23-year-old can make the special throws that separate some of the elite quarterbacks. “Do I think he can make some of the high level throws that I would say the elite guys in the sport right now can make? Mahomes, Allen, Burrow, Lamar, Justin Herbert, Caleb Williams, Matthew Stafford,” Simms said. “Those guys make five or six throws a game where I go, no, you don’t understand there. Nobody in football made those five or six throws today. That was a special play or throw or the ability to kind of slide in the pocket and throw a 25-yard laser on the right sideline into a window where, a lot of quarterbacks, you go, well, don’t even throw that. Don’t even do that. “That’s just one area I think that I’d like to see a little bit more of, and be proven that he can do that on a consistent basis. And I guess I just haven’t seen that yet.” Benefits of playing under center Dart will be asked to play under center much more this season than he did as a rookie. The offense will emphasize play-action throws from the pocket. Dart wasn’t asked to do that often last season, and wasn’t great at it when it was required. Dart completed just 57.3% of play-action passes in 2025, 24th of 26 qualifying quarterbacks, per Pro Football Focus. Early in training camp, Dart said the Giants had “ repped the hell out of ” under center, play-action. It is something we continued to see him spend a large amount of time working on during each practice throughout the summer. Perhaps the under center work is part of helping Dart become “tight and refined” as a quarterback. “I don’t know how much he’s done it [under center], but he looks good doing it. It hasn’t been an issue at all,” Harbaugh said. “I would say, under center in the passing game, it does really discipline your footwork because the drops are so important under center. I think it enhances – he would tell you it helps even in the gun, in the pistol, or whatever. It’s just another element.” Simms believes playing under center, with the increased respect defenses have to give the run game and play-action, will be good for Dart. “The greatest thing is it’s the best way to create explosive plays on the field right now is play action pass,” Simms said. “We’re at an era where it’s very weird, where explosive plays are actually probably at this point, more indicative of who’s going to win the game rather than turnover margin. “So that’s again, where those big throws that we talk about and all that, I think they have more value now in the NFL than ever before, because the defenses are just so good. They’re so talented. It’s too hard to say, Oh yeah, we’re going to drive 12 plays, 75 yards all game long. There’s going to be a strip sack. There’s going to be a tip pass interception. So, you need to be able to make those explosive plays.” Simms said Dart is “made for” the kind of offense the Giants are implementing. There is one caveat. Can he make the difficult throws from the pocket? “Within that play action pass thing, I think we will get to [see] what you’re talking about, where, yeah, we’re going to see if he can make some of those big explosive plays into tight windows, because I think it’s going to be asked of him more this year than it was maybe last year,” Simms said. ‘Best quarterback in the world’ Jon Runyan Jr. spilled the beans regarding an interesting text Dart sent to his offensive linemen a few days ago, per the New York Post . It read: “I want to be the best quarterback in the world.’’ Dart certainly isn’t that right now. He will probably never be. Simms has no issue with the goal. “I have no problems with him telling his teammates and stuff like that,” Simms said “I respect the guy that puts himself out there like that and almost puts pressure on himself and expectations. He lets everybody know. “Your great quarterbacks are all really wired that way … I do respect that confidence and a little bit of the burden of, hey, look, I’m trying to be something special here. So I hope that makes guys want to be a part of that.” It’s no surprise that Simms said Dart won’t get there unless he does a better job protecting himself. “The first thing is you can’t be in the top 10 [among quarterbacks] if you’re hurt every other week,” Simms said. “So let’s just start there. “As you know, the best ability is availability. So, we can’t be taking some of these hits. He’s got to realize that the extra three yards are not worth what his value is to the team. That’s part of being the unselfish quarterback. That’s what you got to do.” Simms believes the talent is there for Dart to be a top 10 quarterback. “I really think he’s got everything,” Simms said. “I just want to see a few more of those in the pocket game-changing difference type of throws.” Sunday’s will be Dart’s first NFL season-opening start. “I think that I’ve just been waiting for this,” Dart said. “I think this is just the coolest stage, the coolest opportunity to play in front of our fans,…

title: NY Giants complete 53-man roster by adding receiver/special teams depth
summary: The New York Giants are completing their 53-man roster by signing wide recever/special teamer Dalen Cambre to the active roster from their practice squad, a source confirms. The move was initially reported by Art Stapleton. The Giants had been carrying just 52 players after releasing wide receiver Darius Slayton earlier in the week. Cambre, a […]
full_text: Dalen Cambre | Getty Images The New York Giants are completing their 53-man roster by signing wide recever/special teamer Dalen Cambre to the active roster from their practice squad, a source confirms. The move was initially reported by Art Stapleton. The Giants had been carrying just 52 players after releasing wide receiver Darius Slayton earlier in the week. Cambre, a former undrafted free agent, played in seven games almost exclusively on special teams for the Giants last season. His presence means the Giants now have five wide receivers on their roster. They are also elevating wide receiver Braxton Berrios from the practice squad to be the punt returner and part of the kickoff unit, and linebacker Malik Harrison. Here is #NYG coach John Harbaugh on 2nd-year WR Dalen Cambre, who had another good day on Wednesday. pic.twitter.com/gg0FqWCuql — Big Blue View (@bigblueview) August 5, 2026 Cambre caught head coach John Harbaugh’s eye early in training camp. “I see him make a circus catch every single day,” Harbaugh said. “And not just that, he’s doing all the other things. He’s doing special teams. He knows what he’s doing. He’s running great routes. I think he’s making a move. I think he’s done a great job and he’s got our attention.” Whether this means anything for Malik Nabers’ availability on Sunday vs. the Dallas Cowboys remains to be seen. The Giants have until 4 p.m. ET on Saturday to announce practice squad elevations.

title: NFL Week 1 betting advice: Giants-Cowboys picks and props
summary: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 1 edition! It’s good to be back. Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! I finished last season a shade over .500, thanks […]
full_text: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 1 edition! It’s good to be back. Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! I finished last season a shade over .500, thanks in part to a perfect 3-0 in Week 18, when the Giants ended their season at home with a decisive win against the Cowboys. Guess what? It’s an immediate rematch! The Giants host the Cowboys this Sunday night to open the 2026 season. That 2025 season-ender was a largely meaningless game for both teams. This time it matters, and it’s John Harbaugh’s long-awaited Big Blue coaching debut. Week 1 is tricky. It’s a brand-new season, and the impact of offseason coaching and personnel changes is an unknown. Sharp bettors can flourish in Week 1, as the markets haven’t always caught up to new trends and realities. But let’s face facts: If this was easy, sports books wouldn’t exist. Dallas and New York missed the playoffs last season, but both have reasons to be optimistic as a new campaign opens. Dallas was dead last in the NFL against the pass in 2025, while New York was second to last against the run. Both teams used the draft and free agency to try to plug those holes. The teams split their games in 2025, with both games going over the total. Dallas won a 40-37 overtime thriller early in the season, and New York prevailed 34-17 in Week 18. Dallas pulled a lot of its starters early in that contest, including Dak Prescott. The trend heading into that final game was ugly for Big Blue – Nine straight losses to Dallas, and 16 of the last 17 in the series. Dallas is favored by 3 points on Sunday, with a game total of 48.5. Let’s get to the picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel . I’ll be honest – I struggled to find three wagers I liked this week. Be careful out there! Game total UNDER 48.5 (-115) . A lot of points were scored both times these teams met last season. But this is Week 1, where defense often has the upper hand while teams shake off the preseason rust. Unders usually do pretty well in Week 1 and are already 2-0 this week. Both defenses should be improved in 2026, and I think this game will be lower-scoring than expected. Cam Skattebo UNDER 69.5 rushing plus receiving yards (-114). This isn’t a high total, but I’m not convinced that Skattebo is going to have a workhorse role and especially right out of the gate. I’m expecting three of the four backs to be active on Sunday night, with all three playing a decent amount of snaps. Jaxson Dart OVER 28.5 rushing yards (-114) . I know the coaching staff wants Dart to protect himself better than he did in 2025, and to be smarter about running. We might see fewer designed runs. That’s all well and good, but getting yards with his legs is a huge part of Dart’s game and is firmly in his DNA as a player. This is a reasonable total for the second-year quarterback, who averaged about 35 rushing yards per game in his rookie season. Questions abound with the Giants’ pass catchers and I can see Dart taking off often. Those are the picks for Week 1. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 1 fantasy preview , with start/sit advice and more, right here.

title: College Football Week 2 – Games and players to watch for the NY Giants
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 2 of the 2026 college football season. The first full week of the 2026 season brought us plenty of fireworks (and more than a little controversy). It also started to confirm for us that this could be one of the most talented draft […]
full_text: Oklahoma defensive tackle David Stone | Getty Images Good morning, New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 2 of the 2026 college football season. The first full week of the 2026 season brought us plenty of fireworks (and more than a little controversy). It also started to confirm for us that this could be one of the most talented draft classes to come out of college in recent memory. This year we’re tailoring our game and player spotlights to the Giants’ needs as they stand right now. And since there’s plenty of season ahead of us, as well as months of draft prep, we’re limiting our focus to one prospect for a game in each time slot. That said, this is a place to discuss all of today’s College Football action. Michigan vs. (11) Oklahoma Fox – noon Spotlight: David Stone (iDL, Oklahoma) If I had to handicap needs for the Giants looking ahead to April, I have to put wide receiver and defensive tackle at the highest priority. So those two positions will figure heavily in our spotlights throughout the year. It helps that this is already shaping up to be an elite receiver class and an excellent defensive tackle class. Stone is probably considered a Top 5 defensive tackle around the NFL, though where he lands will likely depend on the team doing the scouting. He has excellent traits at 6-foot-3, 315 pounds, with (what appear to be) long arms and solid athleticism. He’s explosive off the snap, and while he doesn’t (yet) have great production, he’s effective at blowing up both running and passing plays. Michigan isn’t what they used to be a couple years ago, but they still have strong recruiting and have their share of future NFL players. Controversy surrounding Week 1 aside, this has the potential to be a fun game from a scouting perspective as well as a purely football one. The Giants hope they don’t need to scout quarterbacks, but I have to admit that I’m excited to watch Oklahoma QB John Mateer. Mateer was simply a blast to watch prior to injuring his thumb last year, and makes me think of some kind of horrific Baker Mayfield / Philip Rivers hybrid. Kentucky vs. (12) Alabama ABC – 3:30 p.m. Spotlight: Ryan Coleman-Williams (WR, Alabama) Ryan Coleman-Williams might just wind up being the most polarizing player in this year’s draft class. Still, the Giants are going to have a need at wide receiver after this year, considering they only have four receivers on their roster, and only two under contract after this year. Coleman-Williams is an exceptionally explosive receiver who might wind up running in the 4.2’s. He’s capable of providing instant offense and can take over a game at his best. Unfortunately, he also has maddeningly inconsistent hands and can disappear for stretches when he loses confidence in his mitts. There are obviously plenty of guys on the Alabama squad to watch, but the Giants’ need at receiver, they’ll want to get a good feel for Coleman-Williams. I also want to give a shoutout to Kentucky runner C.J. Baxter. He has great size at 6-foot-1, 227 pounds and the upside to be a solid pass catcher as well as a physical presence out of the backfield. I don’t feel comfortable spotlighting him just yet due to the injury issues at Texas. Still, he’s a former 5-star recruit and a name to watch this year. (4) Texas vs. (1) Ohio State ABC – 7:30 p.m. Spotlight: Hollywood Smothers (RB, Texas) Smothers is our spotlight player, but this game is absolutely crawling with future NFL players. All eyes will be on Texas QB Arch Manning as he looks to redeem last year’s season-opening loss to Ohio State, and from there folks will be paying attention to receivers Cam Coleman and Ryan Wingo. We focused on Ringo last week and he absolutely went off. The Giants hope that they don’t need to look at Arch, and that they’ll be too good to have a chance at Coleman. That brings us to Smothers. The Giants have plenty of power and versatility in their backfield in Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Najee Harris. Smothers gives them the potential home run threat that they don’t currently have in their backfield. It’s notable that John Harbaugh and Greg Roman are known for loving power rushing attacks, but also like to have a speed counter-punch generate big plays. Smothers is undersized at 5-foot-11, 195 pounds, but he’s averaged 6.1 yards per carry for his career and is estimated to have 4.3 or low 4.4 speed. Smothers is also surprisingly tough to get on the ground and 3.99 of his 6.1 yards per carry have come after contact and has forced 74 missed tackles. These are two of the most talented teams in the country, so this is one of those games where my best advice is to watch, enjoy, and take note of anyone who jumps off the screen. I’ll probably be coming back to this game quite a bit during our draft prep.
author: Chris Pflum

title: Three Giants project to be top 50 pass rushers
summary: Quarterback is, easily, the most valuable position on an NFL field. I’ve gone so far as to consider it the foundational position in roster construction, as opposed to merely a “cornerstone” position. By the same token, pass rushers have risen in importance over the last couple years. The ability and traits to win one-on-one and […]
full_text: Abdul Carter | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Quarterback is, easily, the most valuable position on an NFL field. I’ve gone so far as to consider it the foundational position in roster construction, as opposed to merely a “cornerstone” position. By the same token, pass rushers have risen in importance over the last couple years. The ability and traits to win one-on-one and directly disrupt the passer. And in that aspect, the 2026 New York Giants could be sitting on an embarrassment of riches. Seth Walder of ESPN released their projections for the Top 50 pass rushers in the NFL for 2026 this week. All three of the Giants’ edge defenders, Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Kayvon Thibodeaux, project to be among the 50 most productive pass rushers in the NFL. If you consider that defenses want to have two effective pass rushers — in order to keep offenses from easily accounting for a lone pass rusher — then the Giants have three starters. Let’s see what Walder has to say about the Giants’ pass rushers 6. Brian Burns, New York Giants Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.7 2025 sack total: 16.5 Burns has always been a very good pass rusher — and something of a pass rush win rate darling — and exploded for 16.5 sacks in his second season in New York. And the Giants’ pass rush has gotten even deeper. Those 16.5 sacks are enough to launch Burns, 28, into the top 10. But he has a few things working against him. His forecast is negatively affected by only having 8.5 sacks in 17 games in 2024. And while the Giants have a great pass rush, they aren’t expected to be a great team. Middling teams don’t play with a lead as often, which means fewer desperate opponents frequently passing to catch up. Chris’ thoughts Brian Burns is still the “Alpha” on the Giants’ defensive front and is their closer until someone proves otherwise. I see no reason why he should regress as a rusher, considering he added a real power aspect to his usual speed rush. Carter is currently listed as the starter in Dennard Wilson’s defense, but we’ll see plenty of rotation between the Giants’ front 7 players and each of their three edge defenders rushing from unexpected angles. We’ll also see Burns, Carter, and Thibodeaux benefitting from simulated blitzes creating free runs. That said, I suspect Burns’ production will regress slightly from his 16.5 sack season a year ago, but that might have more to do with Carter and Thibodeaux each taking a step forward. Particularly Carter. 22. Abdul Carter, New York Giants Projected mean 2026 sack total: 7.0 2025 sack total: 4 This is a bullish forecast for a player coming off a four-sack season — especially because the model does not explicitly consider draft capital (Carter was the third overall pick in 2025) in its computations. But what it does see is a young player who had a top-10 pass rush win rate. That’s enough to generate a strong number despite being on a below-average team with a defensive coordinator who didn’t blitz much last season. I wouldn’t be shocked if Carter is in the top 10 of the sack leaderboard come January. Chris’ thoughts Carter’s rookie season was an undeniable disappointment, mostly of his own making. He constantly flashed in the first half of the year, but never lived up to his billing. It wasn’t until Mike Kafka got his attention with a pair of benchings that Carter began to really apply himself during the week and started taking over games. In many ways, Carter’s 2025 season reminded me of Jason Pierre-Paul’s 2010 season. That was a disappointment as well, but coming from the other direction as JPP was still figuring out how to even play football. Folks remember how he didn’t produce much until the end of the season, but they tend to forget that he was an absolute demon on special teams all year long. We saw that work on special teams translate to the defense in his second season when he simply took over games and had a DPOY caliber year. I think we can see the same thing this year from Carter. Not only was he Top-10 in win rate, he was 8th in total pressures and led the NFL in quick pressures. That was with half a season of indeterminate effort during the week and simply “out-athlete-ing” NFL athletes as a rookie. After John Harbaugh’s grueling camp, attention to detail, Dennard Wilson’s energy, and Charlie Bullen’s coaching? I’m trying to avoid hyperbole, but I don’t think a “Micah Parsons”, “Young Von Miller”, or “Young Khalil Mack” type season is out of the question. 42. Kayvon Thibodeaux 2026 projected sack total: 5.9 sacks 2025 sack total: 2.5 (10 games) Walder doesn’t offer his thoughts on Thibodeaux, so I’ll just jump to mine. It’s somewhat fitting that Thibodeaux lands right next to Leonard Williams in the sack projection. Like Williams, Thibodeaux is much more of a “complete” defender who has every-down upside, but has largely proven to be better at generating pressure than finishing rushes. That isn’t to say that Thibodeaux can’t finish his rushes. He still finished with 11.5 sacks the last time he was in this style of defense and wasn’t asked to keep contain rather than rush aggressively. Final thoughts Now we’re going to zoom out for a minute before refocusing on Burns and Carter. As Walder points out, the Giants need to put their opponents’ in position where they’re more likely to pass, and then keep the ball in the quarterback’s hands when they do so. There’s been a lot of concern regarding the Giants’ run defense, but I suspect it will see a significant boost under Dennard Wilson. Where Shane Bowen relied on the defensive line to stack and shed blockers while the linebackers hung back at depth, I suspect we’ll see far more stunts and blitzes on run downs. In other words, my guess is that the Giants will be relying on their athleticism up front to shift the math and numbers game in their favor and blow up plays in the backfield, rather than catch them at the second level. Walder also notes that the Giants’ offense might be too mediocre to force opposing offenses to keep up. I’m not so sure. Last year the Giants finished 13th in total yardage and 16th in touchdowns scored. That puts them in the same company as the Los Angeles Chargers and Denver Broncos — two teams with championship aspirations. And that was without Malik Nabers, missing Cam Skattebo for significant periods, and with Wan’Dale Robinson as the Giants’ primary offensive weapon. We don’t know how the Giants’ offense will perform, but it also isn’t like they were the Raiders, Jets, or Browns last year. There are only a few teams with pass rushes that can really rival the Giants’ potential — and that’s not even counting the blitzing upside of Arvell Reese, Micah McFadden or the Giants’ defensive backs. It’s entirely possible that the Giants could wind up with a pair of Top 10 pass rushers if Burns maintains his form from a year ago and Carter takes the expected step forward. Not to mention a potential Top 20 pass rusher if Thibodeaux returns to his 2023 form. I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again, the Giants’ defense could be a lot of fun to watch this year.
author: Chris Pflum

title: New York Giants mailbag: Defensive alignments, expectations as season begins
summary: Richard Vitto asks: I was hoping you could clarify how the defensive line actually gets set up. Most of the time it seems to me that they play only 2 down linemen with 4 linebackers. Maybe to start a game or a possession they use a true front seven but without really tracking I really […]
full_text: Richard Vitto asks: I was hoping you could clarify how the defensive line actually gets set up. Most of the time it seems to me that they play only 2 down linemen with 4 linebackers. Maybe to start a game or a possession they use a true front seven but without really tracking I really don’t think I see it that often. Can you give us a general sense of how often they are in a package with just 2 down linemen and extra dbacks? And when they are on that configuration who are the “starters” most often on the field? Ed says: Richard, I could find and quote you numbers from last season. That, though, is pointless because the Giants have a new defensive coordinator and much different defensive personnel. The “base” defense is considered a 3-4, with three down linemen with their hands in the ground. Again, though, that is kind of pointless. You will see some occasions where the Giants line up that way. You will see occasions where they line up with two down linemen and everyone else standing. You will see occasions where two edge defenders function as hand in the ground defensive ends, making the defense look like a traditional four-man front. You will see times when there is only one true defensive lineman. You will see times when there are none and an edge defender (probably Kayvon Thibodeaux) functions as a pass-rushing nose tackle. Teams play defense nowadays according to down-and-distance, game score, and the game clock. It is all situational. It is impossible to give you numbers on how often different packages are used until we actually see it. That said, the guys I would consider true starters in the front are D.J. Reader, Shelby Harris, Arvell Reese, Tremaine Edmunds, Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Thibodeaux. The safeties are Jevon Holland and Tyler Nubin. Dru Phillips is the nickel cornerback. I couldn’t tell you who the Giants will decided to start at the outside cornberbacks slots — it is some combination of Greg Newsome, Deonte Banks, Paulson Adebo. John Brenner asks: It seems to me that the Giants have developed a troubling pattern over the last 10 or 15 years of not looking ready to play at the beginning of the season. I don’t have the numbers in front of me, but my impression is that they’ve lost the overwhelming majority of their openers and several times they haven’t just lost, but have looked completely unprepared. Do the numbers and your own observations support that impression? If so, what do you think has caused it across different coaches and rosters? And do you see any reason to expect something different against Dallas on Sunday under John Harbaugh? Ed says: John, have you not been reading the website? We have been covering this topic for months. In fact, we have been talking about it for years. I asked Brian Daboll about it before both the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Most recently, it was addressed in this post . Peter Smyth asks: This last week has been fan-torture. I can’t wait for this long, (but hope-filled), offseason to end and find out how good this team really is. National media, and even local writers and hosts are tempering expectations and predict slight or medium improvement. Often, they sound like they haven’t been paying attention to our team and are just writing us off. As a BBV zealot, I have convinced myself the G-men will go on a run this season like Washington in 2024 and the Pats in 2025. I’m asking you to be my Giants-fan-therapist. Am I nuts to strongly think this could be our year? Even a Super Bowl victory? Help me! Ed says: Peter, you are certainly encouraged to be as optimistic as you want to be. Something I keep saying, though, is that the kind of one-year turnaround the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears experienced last season are still the exception rather than the rule. I think if that is what you “expecting” in 2026, you are setting yourself up for disappointment. Maybe it happens. I just wouldn’t expect it to happen. When I made my game-by-game predictions, the most optimistic predicition I could make is 9-8. I still believe that. Maybe the Giants win six games. Maybe everything falls their way, and they get into double-digits in the win column. I feel better about this team because I know the track record of the guy who is now in charge. I just can’t expect an overnight miracle. There is still a lot to be proven, and a lot of work to be done. Doug Mollin asks: Saw a stat from Sharp Football that really caught my eye. “The Giants were leading in games last year for more snaps than the following teams: Ravens, Chiefs, Bengals, Panthers, Vikings, Cowboys, Commanders, Browns, Buccaneers, Saints.” The Giants were leading in games last year for more snaps than the following teams: Ravens, Chiefs, Bengals, Panthers, Vikings, Cowboys, Commanders, Browns, Buccaneers, Saints per @SharpFootball A stat that boggles my mind and should give us hope for better results in 2026 pic.twitter.com/v7k3p66kpc — Justin Penik (@JustinPenik) September 8, 2026 Along with blowing 5 double digit fourth-quarter leads, it really makes me think the Giants could make a bigger leap this year than many expect. Could have had 7 wins last year with a little better luck, better coaching, better execution. What chance do you give the Giants to surprise on the upside over the predicted 7 win total? Is 10 wins out of the question? Ed says: Doug, as I said above, it’s not out of the question. Neither, though, is being a six-win team. As I said above, I just wouldn’t go into the season believing that it is automatic that John Harbaugh is going to turn the Giants into a 13-win team right away. Art Stein asks: To your knowledge is there any exchange of information or knowledge between the Giants and Rutgers. Historically, do coaches from Rutgers ask questions or seek information from the Giants? Ed says: Art, I don’t know what kind of information you think Rutgers coaches might seek from the Giants. To my knowledge, there isn’t anything other than the standard exchange of information about NFL Draft prospects. John McGruther asks: Do you know any of the words which the offense are using for their play calls and instructions, under the new coaching staff? I always remember “Omaha” being heard in the Manning years. Ed says: John, if I did that would be a problem. The rest of the NFL would know them, too. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: NY Giants news: John Harbaugh era set to begin, Matt Nagy, Brian Burns more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the John Harbaugh Era starts tomorrow. John Harbaugh not leaving anything to chance as his Giants era begins | The Record This was the early evening before the New York Giants began training camp at The Greenbrier Resort and John Harbaugh was walking […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the John Harbaugh Era starts tomorrow. John Harbaugh not leaving anything to chance as his Giants era begins | The Record This was the early evening before the New York Giants began training camp at The Greenbrier Resort and John Harbaugh was walking the grounds for the first time. The head coach and several team officials were admiring the picturesque setting with the mountains of West Virginia as the backdrop when someone half-jokingly suggested that the practice fields looked longer than 120 yards. Harbaugh on why Giants were the right fit Harbs Weekly: Time to get a gauge on the Giants | Giants.com Q: That was the start of his era with you, and now the same begins with Jaxson Dart. Where is the line between the importance of the quarterback-head coach relationship and him just being one of 53 on the roster? Harbaugh: To me it’s both, but everybody understands it. He is one of 53. He’s part of the team. He’s a teammate. He’s a player. The guys like Jaxson, Joe [Flacco], Lamar [Jackson], they all understand that so well. That’s why the players love them so much. But the other side of the coin is he’s the quarterback. He’s got to know the most. He’s got to do the most. He has the most impact probably on the game of anybody. So, that part of it is just kind of understood. But those guys, man, they’ve been doing it their whole life. They embrace it. NFC East roundtable: Eagles, Cowboys, Commanders enter critical seasons; Giants seek new culture | The Athletic Who’s the player not enough people are talking about who’s going to make a big impact for the team you cover? Carroll: Isaiah Likely was one of the Giants’ biggest free-agent acquisitions, as the tight end signed a three-year, $40 million deal. That type of deal doesn’t usually lead to a player not being talked about enough. However, in a New York media market adoring the Odell Beckham Jr. reunion, while at the same time fixating on Malik Nabers’ return from a torn ACL, Likely has quietly been putting in the work becoming quarterback Jaxson Dart’s go-to pass catcher. As my colleague Dan Duggan noted, Likely was Dart’s favorite target this summer with 44 catches in 11-on-11 team periods during camp. With or without Nabers’ return in Week 1, Likely figures to be a big piece of this offense. After years of losing, Giants star says, ‘My urgency level is high. This doesn’t last forever’ | NJ.com Given how small an NFL player’s career window typically winds up being, how eager is Burns to win? “Oh, I’ve been at that point…I don’t really give a f— about surprising nobody,” he said. “I’m just focused on our team, our opponents and get a dub as many times as we can throughout the season — and getting to the big dance. Surprising people and putting the world on notice? I don’t give a f— about none of that. Not anymore. “I used to want to prove people wrong and prove this and prove that. But I got to a point where it’s like now, bro, people are going to say something regardless of whether you’re good or whether you’re bad. So it really doesn’t matter. The only thing that matters is the work that’s in front of you. I’m not doing this to prove to nobody else. I do it more so to prove to my guys and myself that we can win.” Giants hope new D-coordinator will be one to finally stop Dak Prescott | New York Post The next coordinator in line is Dennard Wilson, who will be making his Giants debut Sunday and he doesn’t care about Giants-Cowboys history. “We’re going to be unapologetic on how we play,” he said. “We’re going to be decisive in what we do. We’re going to play with an edge. We’re going to play with toughness. We’re going to bring violence. That’s our M.O. title: Eagles News: “Jalen Hurts enters the arena as once again the most polarizing player in the league”
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Here’s where I’m at with Jalen Hurts: I’m not worried about the bottom dropping out with him. It would be shocking if he had a 2020 Carson Wentz season. I tend to think he’ll respond well to the questions about his […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles attempts a pass before a preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Here’s where I’m at with Jalen Hurts: I’m not worried about the bottom dropping out with him. It would be shocking if he had a 2020 Carson Wentz season. I tend to think he’ll respond well to the questions about his future outlook because he thrives when he’s doubted. But in the event that he doesn’t have a good year as the Eagles’ offense struggles, it’s impossible to think that the team will act like that’s no big deal. In that sense, then, there’s pressure for him to play well and secure his next contract extension. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Starting 11: Jalyx Hunt, Jalen Hurts & The Most Fascinating Eagles entering the 2026 season – PHLY Eagles 1) Jalen Hurts. Why did Hurts show us the beauty of that mustache if he wasn’t going to keep it? Better to have ‘stached and lost than never to have ‘stached at all? Tell that to our bandaged hearts. The perception that this is a “make or break” season for Hurts is met with understandable ridicule. This is the Super Bowl MVP we’re talking about. This is the best quarterback in franchise history. But Howie Roseman is beholden to no one. And while the Eagles have proven the constraints of the salary cap to be bendable, it’s true they are staring down the barrel of having or wanting to extend the likes of Cooper DeJean, Quinyon Mitchell, DeVonta Smith, Jalyx Hunt and/or Nolan Smith this offseason. Can you squeeze a $60 million quarterback in there too? Savvy media literates are right to note the degree to which the organization has at the very least been comfortable with the blame for the passing game’s struggles landing on Hurts. There is also a power dynamic at play in which the most powerful person in the organization might bristle at the prospect of Hurts eating into that power too much. Or maybe some people in the front office simply don’t think he’s good enough. If that all sounds like the piling of chips on the shoulder of a person who has made a living and a persona out of turning those chips into fuel, you’re right. After the most radical offseason change of his career, Hurts enters the arena as once again the most polarizing player in the league. Can he make this season undeniable? 6 NFL players with the most to prove in 2026 – SB Nation No. 5: Jalen Hurts, QB — Philadelphia Eagles. I’m really in two minds about including Hurts here, because he’s a very odd case study. Hurts is neither as good as Eagles fans believe, nor is he as bad as 31 other fanbases think he is. Ultimately he’s an above-average QB who is exceptionally good at running Philly’s system, but he’s not elite in comparison with other QBs around the NFL. The “something to prove” factor comes from the weight of expectations. The Eagles are routinely a team that should be contending for Super Bowl appearances with the weight of their roster, so when they fall short it’s only going to raise questions about whose fault that is. One of these has been Hurts’ consistency in the playoffs, where he very often looks like a shadow of himself — and that talk was stoked by A.J. Brown being angered that he wasn’t getting the ball enough. In many ways Hurts has nothing to prove, but he also has everything to prove in 2026. Why Baker Mayfield’s contract means the QB market could burst – ESPN Is he over the Baker Line? For sure. Hurts has been to two Super Bowls and won one. He has a 3.67 touchdown-to-interception ratio in his 10 career playoff games, of which he has won six. You can point out all of the flaws you want, but there’s just no way an organization has the level of success the Eagles have had the past five years if the quarterback isn’t good. If Hurts were in a renegotiation now and demanded to make more than Mayfield, it would be hard to tell him he’s wrong. But this exercise assumes he’ll be in a renegotiation next spring, and there’s no way to know how that will go until we know how this season goes. If Hurts flourishes in the new offense and the Eagles win a ton of games, he’s likely to be in line for something in the $60-plus million range. If he flops and they miss the playoffs, it’s not out of the question to think the Eagles would look to make a change. (Remember how Hurts got the job in the first place, so soon after they had extended Carson Wentz.) If it’s something in the middle — offense starts slow, picks it up late and shows promise, etc. — then Hurts and the Eagles probably figure out some kind of Band-Aid solution that puts off the big decision until after 2027. Fair or not, it feels as if there’s a lot of pressure on Hurts this season to show once again that he belongs at the top of this market. Eagles vs. Commanders preview: 9 things to watch – BGN To me, this looks like a bad offensive line. Based on my correspondences with Hogs Haven this week , Commanders fans seem to think it can at least be a league average blocking unit. Let’s say they’re right. Is average good enough to stop this Eagles front?I have my doubts. Jalyx Hunt had an awesome training camp. He looks ready to make another big leap in his development. Hunt’s stellar summer overshadowed progress made by Nolan Smith, who is healthier than he was last season. A.J. Epenesa and Arnold Ebiketie showed juice as rotational contributors. Jonathan Greenard will NOT play … but the Eagles shouldn’t even need him to be able to generate sufficient pressure from the edge. And then there’s the interior. Jalen Carter. Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo are all poised to have strong seasons. They should be able to generate disruption up the middle, both as pass rushers and run stoppers. This trio contributed to stifling Commanders top running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt (who was limited in practice this week, by the way) last year. 10 Eagles predictions heading into the 2026 NFL season – PhillyVoice 2) The passing game will be up and down all season. The Eagles’ new offense under Sean Mannion is predicated on timing and precision. Run plays must look like pass plays and vice versa. Routes must be run with correct pacing and tempo. And Hurts must adjust to often having his back to the defense while running under center play action. It’s tough enough to master the intricacies of this offense with everyone healthy, but when you add in that DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon missed most of training camp, it could all look pretty choppy for while. On the bright side, the offense will make several improvements from 2025 to 2026. Eli to IR – Iggles Blitz They didn’t fill his roster spot on Saturday. That could mean they will sign Zach Ertz on Monday. The Eagles have talked to Ertz and there seems to be interest from both sides. We’ll find out if that leads to a reunion. They would wait until Monday so that the contract isn’t guaranteed. You normally see multiple teams make moves after Week 1 for that very reason. Stowers isn’t off to the best start with his career. He has missed time due to injury and failed to impress when he did play. Some want to rip the Eagles for taking him in the second round. Some want to label him a bust. I get the frustration with how things have played out to this point. TE isn’t a strength for the Eagles and getting so little from a high pick is disappointing. Our annual look at the Eagles’ top-10 players under 25 years old – NBCSP 6) Darius Cooper [turns 25 Nov. 22]: Along with DeVonta Smith, Cooper is one of only two WRs on the current team who was here last year, and along with Makai Lemon he’s one of only two who are younger than 25. Cooper only caught nine passes last year in limited action, but he’s been so good this summer that everybody in the organization believes he’d be able to contribute…

(Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL season is finally here! The Philadelphia Eagles will get things underway on Sunday afternoon with an NFC East matchup against the Washington Commanders. This is the second year in a row that the Eagles open the season with a divisional game, but they beat the Cowboys in 2025, 24-20, and will look for a similar result against the Commanders. A lot can change in a year, and much of Philadelphia’s offense will look different when Jalen Hurts and Co. take the field on Sunday. The team has a new offensive coordinator, Sean Mannion, who will be up in the booth rather than on the sideline, they’ll be running a completely new system, and have a handful of new skill players to keep an eye on. Head coach Nick Sirianni spoke this offseason about learning a lesson years ago about putting things on film during the preseason, which is why there’s only been hints and suggestions about how, specifically, the offense will differ this year — more plays from under center, more motions and deception. Not even the Eagles defenders would give a peak into how things might look this season, with Cooper DeJean and Jalyx Hunt both being careful not to divulge anything during media availability in the days leading up to the season opener. Luckily for the pair, things aren’t so secretive about the Eagles defense. Back under DC Vic Fangio, a majority of this group has three years together, and some new pieces should take it to the next level. They paid Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter in the offseason, have solid depth at linebacker, and as a whole, are expected to be just as dominant as ever. That doesn’t mean the defense won’t be challenged on Sunday, however. Fangio has to prepare for a new OC in Washington, and he spoke earlier in the week about how difficult mobile quarterbacks, like Jayden Daniels, can make things. Still, the group should shake off any offseason rust quickly, and execute at a high level. The vibes are good in Philly as the Eagles start their journey back to the mountain top. title: Eli Stowers injury: Eagles place rookie tight end on injured reserve
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced two roster moves ahead of their Week 1 home game against the Washington Commanders. Here’s an overview: Note: teams are permitted to temporarily elevate up to two practice squad players per game. A player can be elevated up to three times in the regular season and an unlimited number of […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Eli Stowers #87 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on prior to an NFL preseason football game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced two roster moves ahead of their Week 1 home game against the Washington Commanders. Here’s an overview: TE Eli Stowers was placed on injured reserve. WR Britain Covey was temporarily elevated from the practice squad. Note: teams are permitted to temporarily elevate up to two practice squad players per game . A player can be elevated up to three times in the regular season and an unlimited number of times in the postseason. Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. ELI STOWERS Stowers was limited in practice all week due to a hamstring injury before being questionable to play on Friday’s injury report. Stowers was downgraded to out on Saturday with the Eagles listing him with both hamstring and quadriceps injuries. The Eagles placing Stowers on IR means that the rookie tight end isn’t eligible to return to the active roster until after Week 4. The remaining tight ends on the team: Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, and E.J. Jenkins. The timing of Stowers’ new injury is a bit curious since he told reporters on Friday that he expected to play. Even if Stowers was healthy enough to suit up, it was widely expected that he would be inactive for this game as the fourth tight end on the team’s depth chart. The rookie struggled to make an impact on offense in training camp and preseason games … and he doesn’t exactly offer a special teams background (six total ST snaps over five years of playing college football). By contrast, the Eagles have talked up Jenkins’ ability to contribute in that phase of the game. And so now Stowers will avoid being a healthy scratch, which wouldn’t have been the most flattering look for him or the Eagles since he was a second-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. We’ll see if Stowers is able to get back on the field when he gets healthy. We’ll also see how the Eagles decide to fill the roster spot he leaves behind. ( Zach Ertz return? ) BRITAIN COVEY The Eagles temporarily elevating Covey to the roster for Sunday’s game was widely expected. He figures to serve as their primary punt returner in addition to providing depth at wide receiver. 2026 first-round pick Makai Lemon was also considered to be in the mix to return punts but it looks like that won’t be the case for Week 1. Covey can be temporarily elevated to the roster up to two more times this season.

The confidence comes from the mismatch of the Eagles’ strong defensive front going up against the Commanders’ subpar blockers. Even prior to Laremy Tunsil suffering an injury that could cost him most of this season , Washington was projected to have a below average offensive line: Offensive Line preseason composite ranks, featuring former Browns Scout @sdiben90NFL pic.twitter.com/uU19wzFvXz — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) July 7, 2026 Accounting for the Tunsil loss, the Commanders finished dead last in recent Pro Football Focus offensive line rankings : 32) Before the injury to left tackle Laremy Tunsil, this was a group set to rank just inside the top 20, but the loss of Tunsil for a significant amount of time is a huge blow to the group. There will be an expectation of some improvement from Josh Conerly Jr., and his 59.9 PFF grade in 2025 was fine for a rookie, but this is a unit that could really struggle if Tunsil misses the full season. The Commanders’ starting offensive line configuration looks like this: LT Brandon Coleman, LG Chris Paul, C Nick Allegretti, RG Sam Cosmi, RT Josh Conerly. Coleman was supposed to start at left guard before Tunsil got hurt. Now he’s back at left tackle, where he played as a rookie in 2024. The Commanders were obviously able to have success with him in that role while he ranked 54th out of 87 tackles graded by Pro Football Focus. But Coleman is no Tunsil and now left guard is also worse than they wanted it to be. Offensive line expert Brandon Thorn ranked Allegretti as the worst starting center in the NFL. Cosmi is a good starter. Conerly was a player that I didn’t want the Eagles to draft last year. He struggled as a rookie but there seems to be some hope he’ll improve. To me, this looks like a bad offensive line. Based on my correspondences with Hogs Haven this week , Commanders fans seem to think it can at least be a league average blocking unit. Let’s say they’re right. Is average good enough to stop this Eagles front? I have my doubts. Jalyx Hunt had an awesome training camp. He looks ready to make another big leap in his development. Hunt’s stellar summer overshadowed progress made by Nolan Smith, who is healthier than he was last season. A.J. Epenesa and Arnold Ebiketie showed juice as rotational contributors. Jonathan Greenard will NOT play … but the Eagles shouldn’t even need him to be able to generate sufficient pressure from the edge. And then there’s the interior. Jalen Carter. Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo are all poised to have strong seasons. They should be able to generate disruption up the middle, both as pass rushers and run stoppers. This trio contributed to stifling Commanders top running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt ( who was limited in practice this week, by the way ) last year. Via NFL Pro: Jacory Croskey-Merritt struggled mightily against the Eagles defense in 2025, registering two of his eight lowest success rates (30.8% and 37.5%), two of his three lowest rates of rushing over expected (season-low 15.4% and 25.0%), two of his six fewest yards per carry outputs (season-low 2.2 and 3.1) and two of his eight lowest EPA/carry totals (-0.3 and -0.1) among games where he had at least five rushes. On 21 carries vs. Philadelphia, he generated one explosive run. Washington’s offensive line is already missing its starting left tackle in Laremy Tunsil and […] Nick Allegretti, who is switching over from guard. Jordan Davis led all DT (min. 300 run defense snaps) with a 16.5% run stop rate and 4.3% stuff rate last year, so Croskey-Merritt may struggle to improve upon his marks from his rookie season against Vic Fangio’s defense. Shutting down the run and forcing the Commanders to drop back often should allow Philly’s pass rush to cause problems for Jayden Daniels. 2 – All eyes on Sean Mannion The Eagles led the NFL in three-and-out percentage last year. It was a really bad and boring offense! Kevin Patullo is gone and Sean Mannion is here as the new offensive coordinator. Will the first-time play-caller — who will be operating from the booth as opposed to being down on the field — show promise from the jump? Will this offense be effective after looking uneven in training camp and the preseason games? What do the aesthetics look like in terms of schematics and personnel usage? Any noticeable tendencies? More middle of the field usage? More aggression on the whole? How about the run/pass ratio? Can the Eagles actually avoid getting all of their snaps off with just one second remaining on the play clock? It’s not fair to expect perfection at this point in time but it would be nice to at least see some encouraging signs. Especially since it’s not like the Eagles are facing some juggernaut defense. 3 – Run the ball? Pass? Or both? Looking at Washington’s defense on paper, it’s hard to believe the Eagles won’t be able to find some success against this unit. Which players on that side of the ball should the Eagles be scared by? It’s hardly like they have a bunch of game-wreckers. The Commanders have concerns at cornerback. They’ll be missing projected starter Trey Amos, who is beginning the season on injured reserve. Washington will be starting old friend/Super Bowl LII champion Rasul Douglas and Mike Sainristil on the outside with Amik Robertson working in the slot. Not exactly the most imposing group! Washington Commanders starting cornerbacks: -Rasul Douglas (turned 31 last week, on fourth team since 2023) -Amik Robertson (allowed 817 yards in coverage last season, second most among all corners) -Mike Sainristil (allowed NFL-high 9 touchdowns in coverage last season) pic.twitter.com/cjTyaNT7wN — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) September 3, 2026 The Eagles’ passing attack was very much up and down in training camp, though it sure didn’t help that DeVonta Smith missed most of the summer. Getting him back should help to a significant degree. One would think the Commanders will be trying to focus in on him and dare others to beat them. That much is easier said than done, however, because DeVonta’s a great player. And while there questions about the Eagles’ receivers behind him, the combination of Philly’s talent and Washington’s deficiencies should allow Jalen Hurts to have some level of success moving the ball through the air. If not, the Eagles will be really counting on their run game to come through. It’s the most inspiring aspect of their offense right now and there’s reason to believe Saquon Barkley can have success on Sunday. His four games against the Commanders since the beginning of the Dan Quinn era in 2024: Week 11, 2024 — 26 carries, 146 yards (5.6 average), 2 TD … 2 receptions, 52 yards Week 16, 2024 — 29 carries, 150 yards (5.2 average), 2 TD NFC Championship Game — 15 carries, 118 yards (7.9 average), 3 TD … 1 reception, 4 yards Week 16, 2025 — 21 carries, 132 yards, 1 TD Not bad! Over his entire career, Barkley has owned the Commanders. Through 13 career meetings against them (including playoffs), he’s averaging 103.1 yards per game and 1.2 total touchdowns per game. Of course, the Commanders have a new defensive coordinator now. They’re hoping that Daronte Jones is going to bring some of that Brian Flores secret sauce with him to Landover, Maryland. The burden of proof will be on Jones to prove he can…

title: The Commanders have done a 360
summary: Super Bowl favorites the Rams are the worst team in the league, MVP winner and runners up Matthew Stafford and Drake Maye are the worst QBs in the league, and it’s not even Sunday! Petering out On Sunday the Commanders backup offensive tackle will be either Esa Pole, who was signed to their practice squad […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - AUGUST 14: Head coach Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders looks on before the preseason game against the Miami Dolphins at Northwest Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Super Bowl favorites the Rams are the worst team in the league, MVP winner and runners up Matthew Stafford and Drake Maye are the worst QBs in the league, and it’s not even Sunday! Petering out On Sunday the Commanders backup offensive tackle will be either Esa Pole, who was signed to their practice squad after spending the preseason with the Chiefs; or Trent Scott, who the Commanders liked so much they cut him and signed DJ Humphries, who wasn’t in anyone’s training camp. At cornerback, Rasul Douglas, who was available in July, will start in place of injured Trey Amos. These are pretty important positions to leave to freely available players as primary backups. The Adam Peters/Dan Quinn regime is 17-17, with a point differential of -1. If you want to include the playoffs, they’re 19-18 with a point differential of -16. What is it you say you do here Adam Peters? Since taking over after the 2023 season, the offensive line, even when healthy, isn’t significantly better. The running game still stinks. The defense still can’t stop the run, or the pass. After having the oldest team in the league in 2025, they head into 2026 with the… 6th oldest team. They have the 5th most salary cap space available. Poor drafting, lousy free agent signings, and bad trades brought them right back to where they stared: their fourth double digit loss season in seven years. If this was the state of the Eagles I’d be pissed. Opening Moves Nick Sirianni, far from everyone’s favorite head coach, has yet to lose a season opener, starting his career 5-0 in Week 1. It hasn’t always been pretty, the last four season openers were won by 17 combined points, and they’ve been outgained in three straight. But 5-0 is 5-0. He’s also 6-1 when he has a regular season or playoff bye/week off, with that only loss being his first Super Bowl. 11-1 with extra prep time is a hell of a record. Media darling Dan Quinn, who has the best odds to be fired mid-season (again) is 3-5 in Week 1, and is 5-3 when his team has a regular season or playoff bye, for an 8-8 record when he’s got extra prep time. LeOwner? It is still unbelievable that LeBron James is a Sixer. It’s not a huge surprise though, Rich Paul was constantly talking up the Sixers as an option, and while for basketball reasons it made total sense, at least to me there’s another reason why LeBron would sign: his next job. Would anyone be surprised at all if after his Sixers tenure, unless it goes really badly, that LeBron becomes minority owner of Josh Harris’s teams? I don’t think there is some kind of Aspiration-type shenanigans here. If the Sixers season goes sideways LeBron can cut loose. But it’s Rich Paul’s job to think about what comes next for LeBron. Former Sixers star LeBron James turned Washington Commanders owner LeBron James would be weird. College Football Watch List 12:00 – Oklahoma at Michigan Slightly surprised the AP voters (correctly) dropped Michigan from the top 25. Michigan EDGE John Henry Daley had a breakout season at Utah with 11.5 sacks that ended with an Achilles tear. He’s quick off the snap and has a good set of moves. But he’s also an older prospect, having done a two year mission before enrolling at BYU (then transferring to Utah and then following Kyle Whittingham to Ann Arbor). Interesting day two/three prospect. The Eagles like to take massive OTs on day three. They also like big guards. They’ve also had some luck with an Oklahoma RT. E’Marion Harris , who started his career at Arkansas as a guard, probably a day three pick whose size and versatility can be an asset. 7:30 – Ohio State at Texas We could see this game again in the playoffs. All eyes will be on Arch Manning, but I’m more interested in his receivers. Cam Coleman is the best WR on Texas and Ryan Wingo is potential day two pick. He’s got size and speed, but had issues with drops last year. Ohio State EDGE Kenyatta Jackson has a great physical profile but his pass rushing needs to improve to push him into the 1st round.

title: Eagles News: Sean Mannion is focused on running the ball
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles have an offensive coordinator who really wants to focus on the run game? That’s music to the ears of Birds fans. While I’m feeling unsure about Philadelphia’s offense as a whole, I do have hope for their rushing attack. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Offensive coordinator Sean Mannion of the Philadelphia Eagles talks to Saquon Barkley #26 during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles have an offensive coordinator who really wants to focus on the run game? That’s music to the ears of Birds fans. While I’m feeling unsure about Philadelphia’s offense as a whole, I do have hope for their rushing attack. There were positive signs in the ground game during Eagles training camp. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles notebook: Everything we know about Sean Mannion’s run game going into Week 1 – PHLY The first time Sean Mannion stood in front of the Eagles offensive players, the new coordinator delivered a clear message about where the group needed to begin. “He got up there and said, ‘Our foundation is outside zone,” Eagles right tackle Jordan Mailata said Friday. “Everything is going to start from that.’” After an offseason full of intrigue about what the Eagles’ revamped offense will look like under Sean Mannion, things are starting to come into better focus in the closing days before the season opener against the Washington Commanders. Much of the discourse and scrutiny from afar has come around the pass game. Jalen Hurts’ interception tally became a topic of conversation during training camp as Mannion installed the new system, and the questions about how the former Green Bay Packers quarterbacks coach could get the best out of Hurts has been central over the last few months, as well. But Mannion’s eyes are fixed on what he refers to as, “the engine.” For as much change as this scheme will bring — and there will be plenty as Hurts shifts to being under center more with a focus on outside zone rather than “tight” zone — what won’t change, it seems, is the philosophy from past iterations of this Eagles offense built around the run game first and foremost. “Since he’s been here, he’s put an emphasis on it,” Eagles right guard Tyler Steen said. “Coming from a former quarterback, that’s been pretty cool to see. I think he realizes a lot of the stuff that we do is going to come off the run game, so he wants to put a lot of emphasis on it.” Jalen Hurts talks about his relationship with Philadelphia – BGN As we get closer to the Eagles season opener, Jalen Hurts has been making the rounds and giving interviews, but his recent sit-down with Jason Dumas for 6abc Philadelphia showed that the QB will open up if asked the right questions. Fans want to hear Hurts appreciate the city, and he revealed that he would have a hard time finding the words to explain just how special it is. Eagles-Commanders Final Preview: Jalen Hurts’ Quest For Another Super Bowl Begins NOW | PHLY Eagles YouTube Jalen Hurts is primed to once again be the focus of Philadelphia and the entire football world. As he embarks on a prove-it season without A.J. Brown, with Sean Mannion in charge of the offense and a new cast of wide receivers surrounding DeVonta Smith, it’s time to learn what the league’s most handsome quarterback can do again. Deniz Selman is on hand to help preview what to expect from Washington, Brandon Lee Gowton tells us what he’s watching for on Sunday, EJ Smith checks in from the Eagles facility and Bo Wulf keeps things moving along. A casual fan’s catch-up guide to the Eagles’ offseason – PhillyVoice Makai Lemon is the only player above who is likely to get any real playing time, barring injuries to other veterans on the team. You might ask, “How does he look?” Well, your guess is as good as mine, since we barely saw him, as he was rehabbing a hamstring injury all summer. (In the rare times we did get to see him though… 😬.) Among the guys taken really late in the draft, the most newsworthy selection was native Nigerian Uar Bernard, who had never played a down of football in his life. Fun story, but for the purposes of getting you caught up on this season, he won’t be a factor anytime soon. More Game Talk – WAS at PHI – Iggles Blitz Commanders fans and media members have a surprising amount of confidence in the team. Most outsiders see Washington as one of the worst teams in the league. What gives? The thinking seems to be that Jayden Daniels is healthy and driven to show that he can be the dynamic QB we saw in 2024. They feel the roster is better than 2024, when the team went 12-5 and reached the NFC title game. No one thinks they will win 12 games, but there is a belief the team could finish with a winning record. Washington has two new coordinators and both are doing this for the first time at the NFL level. There are new schemes on offense and defense. The team has already dealt with some injuries, most notably LT Laremy Tunsil. The team didn’t have great depth to begin with and that will start to be really tested as the season goes along. The defense was dead last in yards allowed last year and didn’t make significant upgrades. They added some talented pieces, but I don’t know that they did enough to become a Top 20 defense. Does the offense have enough firepower to win a bunch of shootouts? Basically all this optimism is about Daniels. He sure looked like a special talent as a rookie. He is healthy once again, but that doesn’t guarantee that he’ll have the same level of success. We’ve seen plenty of QBs have a big year and then not match that level in the future. This season will tell us a lot about Daniels. Roob’s Random Observations: Can Eagles earn #1 defense ranking after 45 years? – NBCSP NO. 1 RANKING WITHIN REACH?:” It’s been 45 years since the Eagles had the No. 1 defense in the NFL in terms of points allowed. You have to go back to 1981, when defensive coordinator Marion Campbell’s group allowed just 200 points in 16 games, just 12.5 per game. The Eagles are officially listed allowing 221 points and 13.8 per game, but those numbers include three return touchdowns the Eagles allowed that year. Why the NFL includes return touchdowns in their defensive rankings I’ll never understand. But they do. But that was almost half a century ago, and there have been only three other years the Eagles had the No. 1 scoring defense in the league: 1949 (10.6 points per game), 1950 (10.6 points per game) and 1980 (13.0 per game). They’ve been No. 2 seven times, most recently 2001, 2002 and 2004 under Jim Johnson and 2024 under Vic Fangio. All of which leads us to this year. Can the Eagles earn that No. 1 ranking for the first time since 1981? I don’t see why not. They have the deepest defensive line in the NFL, an all-pro at linebacker, two all-pros at cornerback and a Hall of Fame-caliber coach running the show. The only possible areas of concern are second linebacker, where Jihaad Campbell has a world of potential but is largely unproven, and safety, manned by veteran Marcus Epps and 2nd-year pro Drew Mukuba. But nobody has an all-pro at all 11 spots, and the Eagles are deep and more talented than just about anybody. The defense has six starters who’ve made a Pro Bowl and that doesn’t include guys like Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Jalyx Hunt and Nolan Smith, who are all capable of playing at that level. They can rush the passer, they can stuff the run, they can cover, they can tackle. And most of them have been together for three years and know how to play well together. A big part of earning the No. 1 ranking is having an offense that’s not going 3-and-out all the time and forcing the defense to play too many series and too many snaps. Complimentary football makes things easier on both sides of the ball. So that’s something to keep an eye on because this offense has a lot to prove. We’ll see how that piece of it goes. There are some outstanding defenses in the NFL, starting with DeMeco Ryans’ Texans group, the Broncos, Spags’ Chiefs and the Seahawks,…

(Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers’ ongoing contract dispute with Joey Porter Jr. could be reaching a tipping point. The former second-round pick is not expected to play in the season opener against the Atlanta Falcons. He did not partake in training camp and is still getting “ramped up,” as head coach Mike McCarthy has said. With the season set to begin, though, time has seemingly run out to get an extension done in 2026. The Steelers don’t negotiate contracts during the season, meaning the Steelers would have to use the franchise tag on Porter in 2027 if they wanted to begin negotiations next year. It may not get to that point, though. According to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, the Steelers are open to trading Porter. “The Steelers have been open to listening to offers for Porter,” Schefter and Rapoport report . “But there has not been notable interest at Pittsburgh’s asking price of a premium draft pick — possibly in the first round — and no serious trade talks have developed despite the Steelers’ willingness to deal him.” The Steelers do have depth at the cornerback position, as Asante Samuel Jr had a terrific training camp and preseason. Should he show that he is capable of being the starter, it may make the Steelers more comfortable to seek out trade partners. Let us know what you think in the comments .
